slides.part: Chapter 1: What is a Geographical Indication?
slides.title: Overview
slides.html:
In simple words

A GI is a name or sign on a product that tells you where the product comes from, and tells you that the product is special because of that place.

Think of Darjeeling tea. When you buy a packet marked “Darjeeling”, you expect tea grown on the hills of Darjeeling in West Bengal, with its own light colour and flowery aroma. That flavour comes from the soil, the height of the hills, the cool and misty climate, and the skill of the local tea makers. Tea grown in Assam, Kenya or Nepal cannot become Darjeeling tea, however good it is. So the word “Darjeeling” carries real value, built up by a whole community over more than a century. A GI protects that word, so that only genuine Darjeeling tea can use it.

Your class put the idea in three words: product place linkage. A GI exists only where there is a real link between the product and the place. If the place does not matter to the product, there is no GI.

Some well known GIs: in India, Darjeeling Tea, Kolhapuri Chappal, Banarasi silk sarees, Kanchipuram silk, Kashmir saffron, Basmati rice, Bikaneri Bhujia and Tirupati Laddu; outside India, Champagne, Scotch Whisky, Roquefort cheese and Parmigiano Reggiano.

slides.part: Chapter 1: What is a Geographical Indication?
slides.title: 1.1 Three related ideas: indication of source, GI and appellation of origin
slides.html:
Before the modern GI concept, the law spoke about the origin of goods in older ways. Your notes call the general idea “Indication of Origin”. The easiest way to understand the three ideas is to see them as circles, one inside the other, exactly as drawn in class.

Indication of source (IOS)

Only tells where it was made: “Made in India”

Geographical indication (GI)

Quality or reputation comes from the place

Appellation of origin (AO)

Strictest link to the place, e.g. Champagne, Roquefort

Every appellation of origin is a GI, and every GI also tells you the source. The reverse is not true.

TermWhat it tells youLink with qualityExample
Indication of source (IOS)Only where the product was madeNone. The place does not make the product special.“Made in India” or “Made in China” on a phone or a pen
Geographical indication (GI)Where it comes from, and that its quality, reputation or other characteristic is mainly due to that placeMedium. Reputation alone can be enough. For manufactured goods, at least one stage of making must happen in the place.Darjeeling Tea, Kolhapuri Chappal, Westfälischer Knochenschinken ham
Appellation of origin (AO)Where it comes from, and that its quality is due exclusively or essentially to the natural and human environment of the placeStrongest. In practice the whole product, from raw material to finished good, comes from the area.Champagne, Roquefort cheese

Your notes vs the law

Your notes describe an appellation of origin as a product where “all raw materials, manufacturing process, labour and skill originate from that place”. That is a good way to remember it. The legal test in the Lisbon Agreement (Article 2) is slightly different: the quality and characteristics must be due “exclusively or essentially” to the geographical environment, including natural and human factors.

“Indication of Origin” is a classroom umbrella term. The treaties themselves use the words indication of source, appellation of origin and geographical indication.

slides.part: Chapter 1: What is a Geographical Indication?
slides.title: 1.2 Why does the law protect GIs?
slides.html:
• It protects buyers. Your notes say a GI tag is an “assurance of origin to avoid deception”. A buyer who pays extra for Darjeeling tea should get Darjeeling tea.
  • It stops free riding. The reputation of a GI is built by a whole community over generations. Outsiders should not be able to borrow that reputation for their own goods.
  • It helps producers earn more. Genuine GI goods usually sell at a higher price, and the benefit reaches farmers, weavers and artisans.
  • It protects tradition. Many GIs carry traditional knowledge, skills and culture, such as Toda embroidery or Pattachitra painting.
  • It helps exports. Under TRIPS, other countries need not protect a GI that is not protected in its home country (Article 24.9). India therefore needed its own GI law before it could fight for Darjeeling or Basmati abroad.

slides.part: Chapter 1: What is a Geographical Indication?
slides.title: 1.3 How were such names protected before GI laws?
slides.html:
Your notes say that before GI laws, such products were protected through trade marks and through laws against unfair trade practices. For example, the Tea Board registered the Darjeeling word and logo as certification trade marks under the old Trade and Merchandise Marks Act, 1958, well before India had a GI law. Disputes were also fought through passing off, the common law action against selling your goods as if they were someone else’s.

These routes had weaknesses. A trade mark belongs to one owner, while a GI belongs to a whole community. Passing off needs proof of reputation, misrepresentation and damage in every single case, which is slow and costly. A special GI law gives a community right that is registered once and can be enforced by every authorised producer.

slides.part: Chapter 1: What is a Geographical Indication?
slides.title: 1.4 The Indian definition: four ingredients
slides.html:
Section 2(1)(e) of the GI Act gives the definition. It is long, but it breaks down into four simple ingredients. In any exam answer on GIs, write the definition and then check the facts against these four points.

IngredientWhat it means in simple wordsExample
1. An indicationA name, a geographical or figurative representation (a picture or symbol), or a mix of these, that conveys or suggests where the goods come from (section 2(1)(g))The word “Darjeeling”; the Darjeeling logo
2. GoodsAgricultural goods, natural goods, manufactured goods, handicrafts, goods of industry and foodstuff (section 2(1)(f)). Services are not covered.Tea, rice, silk sarees, chappals, sweets
3. A link with the placeA given quality, reputation or other characteristic of the goods is essentially attributable to their geographical originDarjeeling tea’s flavour comes from its altitude, soil and climate
4. Local activity (for manufactured goods)At least one of the activities of production, processing or preparation takes place in that territory, region or localityKolhapuri chappals are made by artisans in the registered districts

Two more points from class. First, unlike TRIPS, the Indian Act divides goods into categories (agricultural, natural, manufactured, handicraft, industry, foodstuff), while TRIPS simply says “a good”. Second, a GI need not be a place name. The Explanation to section 2(1)(e) says that a name which is not the name of a country, region or locality can still be a GI if it relates to a specific area. Basmati is the classic example: it is not the name of a place, yet it is a registered GI.

Exam tip

Learn the four ingredients by heart: indication, goods, link, local activity. Most GI problem questions are solved by checking these four, then checking the bars in section 9, then checking whether the person using the name is an authorised user.

slides.part: Chapter 2: GI compared with a trade mark
slides.title: Overview
slides.html:
In simple words

A trade mark tells you which business made a product. A GI tells you which place it comes from. A trade mark belongs to one owner; a GI belongs to a community.

slides.part: Chapter 2: GI compared with a trade mark
slides.title: 2.1 The confusing row about generic names
slides.html:
Your table says that under GI law “mostly generic names with location name were protected”, while trade mark law says “generic names can’t be registered”. Here is what this means. A GI usually joins a place name to the ordinary name of the product: Darjeeling + Tea, Kolhapuri + Chappal, Banarasi + Saree. Trade mark law treats such names as merely descriptive and does not like to register them. GI law protects exactly these names.

But neither law protects a name that has truly become generic, meaning a common word for a type of product that no longer tells you where it comes from. “French fries”, for example, no longer means fries made in France. Section 9(f) of the GI Act says such names cannot be registered.

slides.part: Chapter 2: GI compared with a trade mark
slides.title: 2.2 Certification marks
slides.html: A certification mark is a trade mark that certifies that goods meet a standard, for example their origin or quality. The owner certifies other people’s goods, and under Indian trade mark law a certification mark cannot be registered in the name of someone who trades in those goods. The Tea Board’s Darjeeling certification marks are an example. In the United States, Darjeeling tea is protected as a certification mark, because the US uses trade mark law to protect GIs (Chapter 8).

slides.part: Chapter 2: GI compared with a trade mark
slides.title: 2.3 The “Italy and Denmark” Parmesan question from class
slides.html:
From class

Starred in red in your notes: “Italy & Denmark case: is parma cheese a violation of parmesan cheese?”

There is no case with exactly this title. The point the class was making is about genericness: can a famous GI become a common word that anyone may use? Three EU cases explain it.

  • The Parmesan case (European Commission v Germany, EU Court of Justice, 2008). German companies sold cheese as “Parmesan”. The Court held that “Parmesan” evokes the protected Italian name “Parmigiano Reggiano”, so using it for cheese not made to that specification is not allowed in the EU, even if the true origin is shown. Germany could not prove that “Parmesan” had become generic. (The Commission still lost on a procedural point: it had not proved that Germany failed to enforce the protection.)
  • The Feta case (Germany and Denmark v Commission, 2005). Denmark and Germany argued that “Feta” had become a generic name for white cheese in brine. The Court disagreed and upheld Feta as a protected Greek name. This is probably where Denmark comes from in your note.
  • The Parma ham case (Consorzio del Prosciutto di Parma v Asda, 2003). The Court accepted that even the slicing and packaging of Parma ham may be required to happen in the region, to protect its quality and reputation.

Exam tip

For a GI versus trade mark question: define each, use the table, then add one example and one case. The Parmesan case is a good international example of a GI fighting genericness.

slides.part: Chapter 3: How international law protects GIs
slides.title: Overview
slides.html:
In simple words

GI law grew in four steps: Paris (1883), Madrid (1891), Lisbon (1958) and TRIPS (1994). Each step gave stronger protection. India is bound by Paris and TRIPS. India is not a member of Madrid or Lisbon.

TreatyWhat it addedMain weaknessIndia
Paris Convention, 1883First treaty to name indications of source and appellations of origin as industrial property (Art. 1(2)); seizure of goods with false indications (Art. 10 with Art. 9); unfair competition (Art. 10bis)No definitions; covers only false indications; nothing on genericide abroad; remedies depend on national lawMember since 1998
Madrid Agreement, 1891Covers false or deceptive indications; seizure on import (Art. 1); wine names cannot be declared generic (Art. 4)Few members; courts can still declare other names genericNot a member
Lisbon Agreement, 1958 (and Geneva Act, 2015)International registration of appellations of origin at WIPO; a registered name cannot become generic in other member states while protected at home (Art. 6)Only countries with appellation systems joined, so membership stayed smallNot a member
TRIPS Agreement, 1994Definition of GI (Art. 22.1); basic protection for all GIs (Art. 22); stronger protection for wines and spirits (Art. 23); exceptions (Art. 24)Two levels of protection, favouring wines and spiritsBound as a WTO member

slides.part: Chapter 3: How international law protects GIs
slides.title: 3.1 Paris Convention, 1883
slides.html:
The Paris Convention (06/10/26 in your notes) protected industrial property, including industrial and agricultural goods. For GIs, four articles matter.

  • Article 1(2) names “indications of source” and “appellations of origin” as objects of industrial property. This was the first time a treaty used these terms.
  • Article 10 says that the seizure rule in Article 9 applies to goods carrying a false indication of their source. If a country’s law does not allow seizure on importation, it may use other actions and remedies available under its own law (your note: “or any action found suitable by the affected country’s law”).
  • Article 10bis obliges members to protect against unfair competition, meaning “any act of competition contrary to honest practices in industrial or commercial matters”. It gives three examples: acts that create confusion, false allegations that discredit a competitor, and indications that mislead the public about the nature, manufacturing process, characteristics, suitability or quantity of goods. India copied these words into section 22 of the GI Act.
  • Article 19 allows member countries to make special agreements among themselves. The Madrid and Lisbon Agreements were made under this power.

Limitations noted in class: (1) indication of source and appellation of origin are not defined; (2) Article 10 covers only false indications, not merely misleading ones; (3) nothing stops a name from becoming generic in another country; (4) if a country does not allow seizure on importation, the sanctions depend entirely on its national law.

Your notes vs the law

Your notes mention “Art. 11(bis)”. The Paris Convention has no Article 11bis; Article 11 deals with temporary protection for goods shown at international exhibitions. The idea you wrote down, protection against false or misleading indications of source as a way of repressing unfair competition, comes from Articles 10 and 10bis read together, along with Article 10ter, which requires members to give proper legal remedies against those acts.

slides.part: Chapter 3: How international law protects GIs
slides.title: 3.2 Madrid Agreement on false or deceptive indications, 1891
slides.html: Paris members wanted more complete rules, so some of them made the Madrid Agreement (your notes: “created in response to proposal of signatories of Paris for comprehensive regulation”). Its main improvement is that it covers false or deceptive indications, not just false ones. Article 1 requires goods bearing such indications to be seized on importation. Article 4 lets national courts decide which names have become generic, but makes an exception for regional names of wine products, which can never be treated as generic. India is not a party.

slides.part: Chapter 3: How international law protects GIs
slides.title: 3.3 Lisbon Agreement, 1958
slides.html:
The Lisbon Agreement follows the French idea of the appellation of origin: a product whose quality and characteristics are due exclusively or essentially to its geographical environment, including natural and human factors. It works like this:

  • The appellation must first be recognised and protected in its home country.
  • It is then registered at the International Bureau of WIPO, and the other members must protect it.
  • Once registered, it cannot be treated as generic in any member country as long as it stays protected at home (Article 6).

Limitation (from class): it was confined to countries that protected appellations of origin as such, so only a small number of countries joined. The Geneva Act of 2015 extended the system to GIs and allowed bodies like the EU to join; it entered into force on 26 February 2020. India is a member of neither.

slides.part: Chapter 3: How international law protects GIs
slides.title: 3.4 TRIPS Agreement, 1994: the most important treaty
slides.html:
TRIPS is the WTO agreement on intellectual property. It binds India, and the GI Act, 1999 was passed to meet it. Three articles matter.

Article 22: basic protection for all GIs

  • Definition (22.1): GIs are “indications which identify a good as originating in the territory of a Member, or a region or locality in that territory, where a given quality, reputation or other characteristic of the good is essentially attributable to its geographical origin”.
  • 22.2: members must give interested parties legal means to stop (a) use that misleads the public about the origin of goods, and (b) any act of unfair competition under Paris Article 10bis.
  • 22.3: a trade mark that contains a GI must be refused or cancelled if the goods do not come from that place and the use misleads the public.
  • 22.4: protection also applies to a GI that is literally true about the place but still falsely makes people think the goods come from somewhere else. This deals with different places that share a name.

Article 23: extra protection for wines and spirits

  • A wine or spirit GI cannot be used for products not from that place even if the true origin is shown, or the name is translated, or words like “kind”, “type”, “style” or “imitation” are added. So “Scotch like whisky, made in India” is not allowed. Nobody needs to prove that buyers were misled.
  • Trade marks for wines or spirits that contain such a GI must be refused or cancelled for products of a different origin.
  • Where two wine GIs share the same name (homonymous GIs), each is protected, and countries must find practical ways to tell them apart while treating producers fairly.
  • Members agreed to negotiate a multilateral register for wine GIs (your note: “Int’l registers for GI for wines”). These talks have still not finished.

Article 24: exceptions

  • 24.3: a country must not reduce the GI protection it already gave before TRIPS.
  • 24.4: a country need not stop its people from continuing to use another country’s wine or spirit GI if they used it continuously either for at least 10 years before 15 April 1994, or in good faith before that date.
  • 24.5: trade marks applied for, registered or used in good faith before TRIPS applied, or before the GI was protected at home, are not affected.
  • 24.6: no protection is needed for a term that is the common name of the goods in that country, or for grape variety names.
  • 24.7: a country may set a time limit of five years for challenging a trade mark that conflicts with a GI, unless there is bad faith. India copied this in section 26(4).
  • 24.8: people may use their own name in trade, unless it misleads.
  • 24.9: there is no obligation to protect a GI that is not protected, or has fallen into disuse, in its home country.

Your notes vs the law

Your note on Article 24(4) says “10 years before April 1994 in good faith”. The actual text gives two separate options: use for at least 10 years before 15 April 1994, or good faith use before that date. Either one is enough.

How India copied TRIPS. Seeing the match makes the Indian Act much easier to remember.

slides.part: Chapter 3: How international law protects GIs
slides.title: 3.5 The two level problem and India’s demand
slides.html: TRIPS gives wines and spirits much stronger protection than everything else. For other products, the owner must show that the use misleads the public or is unfair competition. This suits Europe, which has thousands of wine and spirit names, but not India, whose famous GIs are tea, rice, textiles and handicrafts. India has therefore long supported extending Article 23 level protection to all products, so that names like Basmati and Darjeeling get the same strong protection as Champagne. This issue is still unresolved at the WTO.

slides.part: Chapter 3: How international law protects GIs
slides.title: 3.6 The grandfather clause
slides.html:
A grandfather clause lets an existing user carry on even though new users are banned. In GI law it appears in TRIPS Article 24.4 (old users of wine and spirit names), Article 24.5 (old good faith trade marks), and the 2006 wine agreement between the EU and the US (Chapter 4).

Your notes vs the law

Your notes say “Prefixes + GI = allowed TM” and “Uncle Sam + Scotch Whiskey = Allowed”. Use this only as a memory aid for the idea of grandfathering. As a statement of law it is not correct: Article 23.1 bans using a spirit GI on other spirits even with extra words added, so a prefix does not make it lawful. Continued use is allowed only if an exception applies, such as long prior use or a prior good faith trade mark. The EU and US agreement covers wine names only, and US rules recognise Scotch whisky as a distinctive product of Scotland.

Exam tip

For a question on international GI protection, go in order: Paris, Madrid, Lisbon, TRIPS. Say what each added and what its weakness was. End with the two level problem and India’s demand for extension.

slides.part: Chapter 4: The 2006 US and EU wine agreement: semi generic names
slides.title: Overview
slides.html:
In simple words

In the US, some famous European wine names, such as Champagne, Chablis and Sherry, had become everyday words for types of wine. In 2006 the US agreed to stop new uses of these names on non EU wine, but allowed old labels to continue. This is the grandfather idea in action.

slides.part: Chapter 4: The 2006 US and EU wine agreement: semi generic names
slides.title: 4.1 What is a semi generic name?
slides.html:
A semi generic name is a name that still has geographic meaning but is also used in the US as the name of a class or type of wine. The slides list 16 such names: Burgundy, Chablis, Champagne, Chianti, Claret, Haut Sauterne, Hock, Madeira, Malaga, Marsala, Moselle, Port, Rhine, Sauterne, Sherry and Tokay. Retsina, a Greek type of wine, is not a semi generic name, but the agreement treats it the same way.

Even before the agreement, US law allowed a semi generic name on wine from elsewhere only if the true place of origin appeared right next to it (for example “California Champagne”) and the wine met the standard for that type.

slides.part: Chapter 4: The 2006 US and EU wine agreement: semi generic names
slides.title: 4.2 What the agreement did
slides.html:
• The agreement was signed on 10 March 2006.
  • The US promised to change its law so that these names may be used only on wine from the relevant EU country.
  • Grandfather exception: anyone already using such a name on a label approved before 10 March 2006 may continue, but only on labels carrying the same brand name, or the same brand name and the same fanciful name, shown on that approval. The approval is called a COLA, a Certificate of Label Approval, issued by the US Alcohol and Tobacco Tax and Trade Bureau (TTB).

slides.part: Chapter 4: The 2006 US and EU wine agreement: semi generic names
slides.title: 4.3 The Smith example from the slides
slides.html:
Company A sells “Smith Elegance California Cream Sherry”. On its COLA, the brand name is “Smith”, the fanciful name is “Elegance”, the class and type is “Sherry”, and the appellation of origin is “California”.

What Company A changesCan it still use “Sherry”?Why
Brand name Smith becomes JonesNoA new brand is a new label, so the old right does not carry over
Fanciful name Elegance becomes RobustNoThe fanciful name must stay the same
Appellation California becomes Napa ValleyYesOnly the brand and fanciful names are frozen; the stated origin can be updated
Drops the word “Cream”YesThis does not change the brand or fanciful name
Sells the brand to Company BYes, with the same limitsThe right follows the brand, so Company B and any later owner get the same rights and restrictions

Exam tip

Use this agreement as your example of grandfathering. The key point: the protection follows the label (brand name), not the company. Change the brand or fanciful name and the right is lost.

slides.part: Chapter 5: The Indian GI Act, 1999: how the system works
slides.title: Overview
slides.html:
Full name: the Geographical Indications of Goods (Registration and Protection) Act, 1999 (Act 48 of 1999). It came into force on 15 September 2003, together with the GI Rules, 2002. The GI Registry is in Chennai, and the Registrar of GIs is the Controller General of Patents, Designs and Trade Marks. The first application was for Darjeeling Tea, filed by the Tea Board on 27 October 2003, and Darjeeling Tea became India’s first registered GI in 2004 to 2005. Your notes record the Act as India’s step to comply with TRIPS.

In simple words

A producers’ body registers the GI name. Individual producers then register as authorised users. Only authorised users may use the name. Registration lasts 10 years and can be renewed forever. The name can never be sold or licensed. Misuse can be stopped by a civil suit, and it is also a crime.

slides.part: Chapter 5: The Indian GI Act, 1999: how the system works
slides.title: 5.1 Who can apply?
slides.html:
Not an individual. Section 11(1) allows an application only by an association of persons or producers, or an organisation or authority set up under any law, that represents the interest of the producers of the goods.

The class asked: who is the producer whose interest must be represented? Section 2(1)(k) answers it.

Type of goodsWho counts as a producer
Agricultural goodsA person who produces the goods, including one who processes or packages them
Natural goodsA person who exploits them (for example, extracts or collects them)
Handicraft or industrial goodsA person who makes or manufactures them
All of the aboveAlso includes anyone who trades or deals in that production, exploitation, making or manufacturing

Government bodies as proprietors (class). Many GIs are held by statutory bodies, for example the Tea Board (Darjeeling Tea), APEDA (Basmati), and the leather development corporations of Maharashtra and Karnataka, LIDCOM and LIDKAR (Kolhapuri Chappal). Your notes also list the Coffee Board, the Spices Board and a Horticulture Board. The Toda Embroidery case (Chapter 6) shows that the real question is always whether the applicant represents the producers.

Your notes vs the law

The EU allows a single producer to apply in some cases (your notes: “even a single person producing a certain handicraft can file”). India does not. Under section 11, the applicant must always be a body representing the producers.

slides.part: Chapter 5: The Indian GI Act, 1999: how the system works
slides.title: 5.2 Two kinds of registered persons: Part A and Part B of the Register
slides.html:
The Register of GIs (section 6) has two parts (section 7):

Part APart B
The GI itself and its registered proprietorThe authorised users
The association or authority that filed the applicationIndividual producers of the area who apply and are registered to use the GI
Example: the Tea Board for Darjeeling TeaExample: the individual tea gardens of Darjeeling

Think of the proprietor as a trustee who holds the name for the community, and the authorised users as the people who actually use it. Your notes put it well: proprietors are not direct beneficiaries; they are the channel through which the benefit percolates into the community, and the proprietor by itself is not responsible for maintaining quality.

A producer becomes an authorised user by applying under section 17. Producers named in the original application can be registered together with the GI. An authorised user’s registration lasts 10 years, or until the GI registration ends if that is earlier, and it can be renewed.

slides.part: Chapter 5: The Indian GI Act, 1999: how the system works
slides.title: 5.3 What the application must contain
slides.html:
Section 11(2) and Rule 32(6) of the GI Rules list what must be included. In simple words:

  • A statement explaining how the GI shows that the goods come from the area, and how their special quality, reputation or other characteristic is due exclusively or essentially to the area’s natural and human factors.
  • The class of goods.
  • A map of the area, with three certified copies.
  • How the GI looks: words, a figurative element (a logo), or both.
  • Particulars of the producers to be registered at the start.
  • An affidavit explaining how the applicant represents the producers.
  • A standards benchmark: the standards for producing or making the goods, and details of any human creativity involved.
  • The mechanism for maintaining quality, integrity and consistency among producers.
  • Details of special human skill or the uniqueness of the geographical environment.
  • The full name and address of the applicant body.
  • Details of the inspection structure, if any, that will control use of the GI.
  • For a homonymous GI, the factors that distinguish it from the already registered GI and the steps taken to protect consumers from confusion.

A single application can cover several classes of goods, with a fee for each class (section 11(3)).

From class

“Reliance’s GI for petroleum products: ISO standards cannot be a benchmark.” No record of such an application or decision could be found, so treat it as a classroom illustration. The principle behind it is sound: Rule 32(6)(b) asks for standards that show the place linked quality of the goods. A general international standard such as ISO measures uniform industrial quality, not something that comes from a place, so on its own it cannot prove the link a GI needs.

“Basmati Rice Case”, written next to the rule on quality control, shows why defining the area and the standards matters so much (Chapter 6).

slides.part: Chapter 5: The Indian GI Act, 1999: how the system works
slides.title: 5.4 What cannot be registered as a GI
slides.html:
Section 9 (headed “What cannot be a GI!” in your notes) bars seven kinds of indications. Grouped simply:

BarMeaningClassroom link
1. Deceptive or confusingIts use would be likely to deceive or cause confusionA name that suggests the wrong origin
2. Against the lawIts use would be contrary to any law in forceMahua Taadi, Bhaang Thandai, Meghalaya bird feather cap
3. Scandalous or obsceneIt contains scandalous or obscene matterOffensive names
4. Hurts religious feelingsIt contains matter likely to hurt the religious susceptibilities of any class or section of citizensThe Tirupati Laddu debate
5. Not protectable in a courtIt would otherwise be disentitled to protection in a court“(Prasad)” in your notes
6. Generic or not protected at homeA generic name, or a GI that is not protected, has stopped being protected, or has fallen into disuse in its home country“French fries” type names; foreign GIs that are dead at home
7. Literally true but misleadingTrue about the place, but falsely suggests that the goods come from another placePlaces that share the same name

Genericness test. In deciding whether a name has become generic, the Registry looks at the situation both in the place where the name originated and in the area where the goods are consumed (Explanation to section 9).

Your notes vs the law

Your notes link “Mahua Taadi, Bhaang Thandai, Meghalaya bird feather cap” to the bar on illegality. No GI application or refusal could be found for any of these, so use them only as illustrations: mahua liquor may clash with state excise laws, bhang with the Narcotic Drugs and Psychotropic Substances Act, 1985 where state law does not allow it, and caps made from the feathers of protected birds with the Wild Life (Protection) Act, 1972.

Can a temple prasadam be a GI? Your notes ask this about the Tirupati Laddu. It is in fact registered (2009). A challenge argued that a religious offering is not “goods” and that registration hurts religious feelings, but it failed because the challenger was not a “person aggrieved”. So no court or Registry has decided the religious question on its merits (Chapter 6). In an exam, argue both sides: the laddu is made with a set recipe, special skill and a reputation tied to Tirumala; but it is a religious offering made by a single body, which sits uneasily with the community idea behind GIs and with section 9(d).

slides.part: Chapter 5: The Indian GI Act, 1999: how the system works
slides.title: 5.5 Homonymous GIs
slides.html:
Homonymous GIs are GIs that are spelt or sound the same but belong to different places. Section 10 allows such a GI to be registered if the Registrar is satisfied about three things:

  • There are practical conditions that will keep the two GIs apart, for example clear labels showing the region.
  • The producers of both places are treated fairly (equitably).
  • Consumers will not be confused or misled.

Rule 32(6)(h) supports this by asking the applicant to explain the differences and the protective measures. A simple way to picture it: two regions in two different states share the same name, and each is known for its own type of shawl. Both GIs can be registered if the labels make clear which region each shawl comes from.

slides.part: Chapter 5: The Indian GI Act, 1999: how the system works
slides.title: 5.6 The registration process step by step
slides.html:
Your notes for 13/10/26 have the heading “Registration Process” with Part A and Part B left blank. Here is the full process.

Application filed at the GI Registry, Chennai, by the producers’ body, with the statement of case, map, list of producers and fee

↓

Preliminary scrutiny: the Registry checks for gaps and asks for corrections

↓

Examination, including review by a consultative group of experts who test the claims about the place and the product

↓

Objections and hearing if needed, then acceptance (with or without conditions) or refusal, with reasons

↓

Advertisement in the GI Journal

↓

Opposition by any person within 3 months, extendable by up to 1 more month

↓

The applicant files a counter statement within 2 months, or the application is treated as abandoned; evidence and a hearing follow

↓

Registration and certificate; the GI counts as registered from the date of application

↓

Producers apply to become authorised users (Part B)

↓

Renewal every 10 years

Fees today. The GI (Amendment) Rules, 2025, notified on 3 November 2025, cut the application fee from ₹5,000 to ₹1,000 per class and the renewal fee from ₹3,000 to ₹500.

slides.part: Chapter 5: The Indian GI Act, 1999: how the system works
slides.title: 5.7 How long protection lasts
slides.html: A GI registration lasts 10 years and can be renewed for 10 years at a time, without any limit (section 18). A late renewal is possible within six months of expiry with an extra fee, and a GI removed for non renewal can be restored on application.

slides.part: Chapter 5: The Indian GI Act, 1999: how the system works
slides.title: 5.8 Quality control: India compared with the EU
slides.html:
Your notes for 27/10/26 make an important practical point.

IndiaEuropean Union
The Registry examines the goods only against the specifications in the applicationThe whole process from scratch is examined against a detailed product specification
The method of cultivation usually does not matter, for example organic or chemical farming of Basmati, natural or synthetic dyes for PattachitraInputs matter, for example milk quality and cow fodder for cheese
The application only has to describe the inspection structure “if any”A named control body must check compliance; controls are a condition of registration

Critical point: weak checking after registration is one of the main criticisms of the Indian system. A GI tag is only as good as the quality control behind it.

slides.part: Chapter 5: The Indian GI Act, 1999: how the system works
slides.title: 5.9 What rights registration gives
slides.html:
• The registered proprietor and the authorised users can sue for infringement (section 21(1)(a)).
  • Authorised users get the exclusive right to use the GI on the registered goods (section 21(1)(b)), subject to any conditions entered on the register (section 21(2)).
  • Where there are several authorised users, none of them can stop the others merely because of registration; each has the same rights against outsiders (section 21(3)).
  • The registration certificate is prima facie evidence that the GI is valid (section 23).
  • An unregistered GI cannot be the basis of an infringement suit (section 20(1)), but a passing off action is still possible (section 20(2)). The Scotch Whisky case used this route.

slides.part: Chapter 5: The Indian GI Act, 1999: how the system works
slides.title: 5.10 A GI can never be sold or licensed
slides.html:
Section 24 says a GI cannot be the subject of assignment, transmission, licensing, pledge, mortgage or any similar agreement. The reason is simple: a GI belongs to a place and its community, not to a company. The only exception is death: when an authorised user dies, the right passes to the successor in title.

This is a key difference from trade marks, and it settled one argument in Tea Board v ITC. The Tea Board said ITC should have taken a licence, but the court pointed out that a GI cannot be licensed at all.

slides.part: Chapter 5: The Indian GI Act, 1999: how the system works
slides.title: 5.11 Infringement: what counts as misuse
slides.html:
A person who is not an authorised user infringes a registered GI in three main ways (section 22(1)):

  • Misleading use about origin (22(1)(a)): using the GI, or anything that suggests it, so that buyers are misled about where the goods come from. Example: selling Nepal tea as “Darjeeling”.
  • Unfair competition, including passing off (22(1)(b)): any act contrary to honest practices in industrial or commercial matters. The Act lists three types: creating confusion with a competitor, false statements that discredit a competitor, and use that misleads about the nature, manufacturing process, characteristics, suitability or quantity of the goods. This comes straight from Paris Article 10bis.
  • Literally true but misleading (22(1)(c)): using another GI that is true about its own place but makes buyers think the goods come from the area of the registered GI. Your note “same place, same product, one GI, one non GI” refers to this situation: a true name used in a way that lets a non GI product pass as the GI product.

slides.part: Chapter 5: The Indian GI Act, 1999: how the system works
slides.title: 5.12 Extra protection for notified goods
slides.html:
Sections 22(2) and 22(3) are India’s version of TRIPS Article 23, with one difference: India can give this extra protection to any goods, not only wines and spirits. The Central Government must first notify the goods. For notified goods, it is infringement to use another GI on goods not from that place even if the true origin is shown, the name is translated, or words like “kind”, “style” or “imitation” are added. Section 25(b) also bars trade marks containing a GI for notified goods.

Your notes vs the law

Your notes give “Kolhapuri style Chappal, Banarasi type silk” as examples under section 22(3). Be careful. The extra protection applies only to notified goods, and the only notification found (S.O. 2401(E), dated 1 October 2010) covers wines and spirits alone. Research published in 2019 and 2022 also found that no other goods had been notified.

So “Kolhapuri style chappal” does not automatically infringe under section 22(3). It can still be challenged under section 22(1) if it misleads buyers or amounts to unfair competition, but then the proprietor must prove that.

This is a well known criticism: India argued at the WTO for stronger protection for all products, yet has used its own power only for wines and spirits.

slides.part: Chapter 5: The Indian GI Act, 1999: how the system works
slides.title: 5.13 Reselling genuine goods is allowed
slides.html: Section 22(4) is the rule of exhaustion. If someone lawfully buys genuine GI goods, they can resell them, process them or repack them without infringing, unless the condition of the goods is impaired after they were put on the market. A shop repacking genuine Darjeeling tea into smaller packets is fine; a shop mixing it with cheaper tea and still calling it Darjeeling is not.

slides.part: Chapter 5: The Indian GI Act, 1999: how the system works
slides.title: 5.14 GIs and trade marks: the special rules
slides.html:
Chapter V of the Act (“special provisions relating to trade marks and prior users”) balances GIs against existing trade marks.

  • Section 25: the Registrar of Trade Marks must, on his own or at the request of an interested party, refuse or cancel a trade mark that contains a GI for goods not from that place where the use would mislead, or that contains a GI for notified goods.
  • Section 26(1): a trade mark containing a GI that was applied for, registered or used in good faith before the Act came into force, or before the GI application was filed, stays valid.
  • Section 26(2): the Act does not apply to a term that was the common name of the goods in any part of India on or before 1 January 1995.
  • Section 26(3): a person may use their own name, or the name of their predecessor in business, unless it confuses or misleads.
  • Section 26(4): the five year limit, marked “Very imp” in your notes, explained below.

The five year limit in simple words. No action can be taken against the use or registration of a trade mark after five years from whichever of these comes first:

  • the date the GI proprietor or authorised user came to know of the infringing use or registration; or
  • the date the trade mark was registered, provided it had been published by then.

This protection is lost if the trade mark was used or registered in bad faith. The rule comes from TRIPS Article 24.7, and Tea Board v ITC shows it in action: the Tea Board knew of “Darjeeling Lounge” from 2005 but sued only in 2010, and lost.

Exam tip

Quote section 26(4) in any question about a trade mark that uses a GI. Then check three things: when the GI owner learnt of the use, when the trade mark was registered, and whether there was bad faith.

slides.part: Chapter 5: The Indian GI Act, 1999: how the system works
slides.title: 5.15 Remedies: civil and criminal
slides.html:
Civil remedies. An infringement or passing off suit must be filed in a District Court or a higher court (section 66). The court can grant an injunction (including a temporary one), damages or an account of profits (at the plaintiff’s choice), and order delivery up of infringing labels and goods for destruction (section 67). If the defendant acted innocently and stopped as soon as they knew of the GI, only nominal damages are given.

Criminal penalties. Your notes for 28/10/26 have the heading “Penalities” with nothing written below it. Here are the main offences:

OffencePunishment
Falsifying a GI, or falsely applying it to goods (section 39)Imprisonment from 6 months to 3 years and a fine from ₹50,000 to ₹2 lakh, unless the accused proves there was no intent to defraud; the court may give less for adequate and special reasons
Selling, hiring or keeping for sale goods with a false GI (section 40)The same punishment. Defences: reasonable precautions were taken, the supplier is disclosed, or the accused acted innocently
Second or later conviction (section 41)Imprisonment from 1 to 3 years and a fine from ₹1 lakh to ₹2 lakh
Falsely representing a GI as registered (section 42)Up to 3 years, or a fine, or both
Falsely suggesting a business is connected with the GI Registry (section 43)Up to 2 years, or a fine, or both
Falsifying entries in the register (section 44)Up to 2 years, or a fine, or both

Offences under sections 39 to 41 are cognizable. A police officer not below the rank of Deputy Superintendent may search and seize without a warrant, but must first obtain the Registrar’s opinion and act on it. A prosecution must start within three years of the offence or two years of its discovery, whichever ends first.

slides.part: Chapter 5: The Indian GI Act, 1999: how the system works
slides.title: 5.16 Rectification and appeals
slides.html:
Any person aggrieved can apply to cancel or correct an entry in the register, for example because a GI was wrongly registered or a condition was broken (section 27). Who counts as a person aggrieved matters: the Tirupati Laddu challenge failed on exactly this point.

Appeals from the Registrar used to go to the Intellectual Property Appellate Board (IPAB). The Tribunals Reforms Act, 2021 abolished the IPAB, and appeals and rectification matters now go to the High Court.

slides.part: Chapter 5: The Indian GI Act, 1999: how the system works
slides.title: 5.17 Where India stands today
slides.html:
• Number of GIs: reports based on GI Registry data put the figure at 822 registered GIs as of 31 March 2026, with handicrafts the largest group.
  • Common GI logo: your notes say a GI logo is used uniformly across all GIs. The logo and the tagline “Invaluable Treasures of Incredible India” were launched on 1 August 2018. Under DPIIT guidelines issued in 2019, registered Indian GIs may use them with permission, free of charge; foreign GIs may not. The logo is a branding tool, not a legal requirement under the Act.
  • Lower fees since November 2025 (see 5.6).

slides.part: Chapter 6: The important GI cases
slides.title: Overview
slides.html: Your notes say “Cases: refer ppt shared by ma’am” and list Tea Board v ITC, the Scotch Whisky case, Chinar Agro Fruit (the Champagne case) and Bikaji Foods v Desai Brothers. They also mention Toda Embroidery, the Tirupati Laddu, Basmati and the Prada Kolhapuri controversy. Each case below follows the same pattern: story, question, decision, lesson.

slides.part: Chapter 6: The important GI cases
slides.title: Tea Board, India v ITC Limited (the Darjeeling Lounge case)
slides.html:
Court

Calcutta High Court. Interim order on 20 April 2011 (Justice Sanjib Banerjee). Final judgment on 4 February 2019 (Justice Sahidullah Munshi).

Story

The Tea Board holds the GI and certification trade marks for “Darjeeling”. ITC runs the ITC Sonar hotel in Kolkata and named a lounge, where food and drinks are served, “Darjeeling Lounge”. ITC also applied to register “Darjeeling Lounge” as a trade mark.

Question

Does naming a hotel lounge “Darjeeling Lounge” infringe the Darjeeling GI and certification marks, or amount to passing off or unfair competition?

Decision

The court said no, for three reasons:

  1. Time bar: the suit was barred by the five year limit in section 26(4), because the Tea Board knew of the use from 2005 but sued only in 2010.
  2. Goods, not services: the GI covers tea, which is goods, while a lounge is a service. The certification mark, registered under the old 1958 Act, also covered goods only.
  3. No confusion: guests would not think the lounge was licensed by the Tea Board or that everything served there came from Darjeeling; the two businesses are different.

The suit was dismissed with costs of ₹1 lakh.

Lesson

A GI is tied to goods, it is not a monopoly over a place name, and the five year limit is strict.

Exam tip

slides.part: Chapter 6: The important GI cases
slides.title: Scotch Whisky Association v Golden Bottling Ltd (the Red Scot case)
slides.html:
Court

Delhi High Court, 20 April 2006 (Justice Madan B. Lokur).

Story

Golden Bottling sold Indian whisky under the name “Red Scot”. The Scotch Whisky Association and member distillers objected that “Scot” suggested Scotch whisky, which under UK law must be made in Scotland.

Question

Can the use of “Red Scot” for Indian whisky be stopped, even though Scotch whisky was not a registered GI in India at the time?

Decision

Yes. Relying on the UK Scotch Whisky Act, 1988 and the Scotch Whisky Order, 1990 to show what “Scotch” means, the court held that the use amounted to passing off and restrained the defendant.

Lesson

Even an unregistered GI can be protected through passing off. Section 20(2) of the GI Act keeps this route open.

slides.part: Chapter 6: The important GI cases
slides.title: Comité Interprofessionnel du Vin de Champagne v Chinar Agro Fruit Products (the Champagne case)
slides.html:
Court

Delhi High Court, 7 September 2017 (Justice Sanjeev Sachdeva).

Story

The Comité Interprofessionnel du Vin de Champagne (CIVC), the French body representing Champagne producers, holds an Indian GI registration for CHAMPAGNE for wine (registered in 2008). Chinar Agro Fruit Products sold non alcoholic sparkling drinks, fruit beer and juices under the name “Champagne”.

Question

Can a registered foreign GI for wine stop the use of the name on non alcoholic drinks?

Decision

Yes. The defendant did not appear, so the suit went ahead ex parte, and the court granted a permanent injunction against using “Champagne” or anything suggesting a link with the Champagne region. CIVC had argued infringement under section 22, passing off, and the danger of the name becoming generic in India.

Lesson

Foreign GIs registered in India get full protection, even against a different kind of goods. Because the decree was ex parte, it carries less weight as a precedent on points that were never argued.

slides.part: Chapter 6: The important GI cases
slides.title: Bikaji Foods International Ltd v Desai Brothers Ltd (the Bikaneri Bhujia case)
slides.html:
Court

Delhi High Court, CS(COMM) 695/2023, interim orders of 5 and 11 October 2023.

Story

Bikaji Foods, a snack maker from Bikaner, relied on the GI “Bikaneri Bhujia” and its own trade mark BIKAJI. It objected to the packaging of Desai Brothers’ “Pitaara Bikaneri Bhujia”.

Question

Was the defendant misusing the GI and copying the packaging? Was its bhujia actually made in Bikaner?

Decision

At the interim stage, the court directed the defendants to adopt clearly different packaging, required a clear distinction between GI and non GI products, and appointed a Local Commissioner to check whether Bikaneri Bhujia was really being made at the defendants’ premises in Bikaner.

Lesson

Where the goods are actually made is the key fact in GI use, and courts will police the line between GI and non GI products. These were interim orders; no final judgment was found.

slides.part: Chapter 6: The important GI cases
slides.title: Toda Embroidery (who represents the community?)
slides.html:
Forum

GI Registry (application filed in 2008, registered in 2013).

Story

The Todas are a tribal community of the Nilgiris in Tamil Nadu, known for their red and black embroidery. A GI application for Toda Embroidery was filed in 2008 by the Toda Nalavaazhvu Sangam (TNS), a society of Toda community members, and the Keystone Foundation (KF), a trust working with Toda craftswomen. The application was advertised, and objections followed.

Question

Did TNS and KF really represent the interest of the Toda producers, as section 11(1) requires?

Decision

Yes. Your notes record the holding: they did represent the community, and the GI was registered.

Lesson

Under section 11, the question is whether the applicant represents the producers, not whether it is itself a producer. A body such as an NGO working with the community can be a proper applicant.

slides.part: Chapter 6: The important GI cases
slides.title: Tirupati Laddu (can a temple offering be a GI?)
slides.html:
Forum

GI Registry, with a public interest petition in the Madras High Court.

Story

Tirumala Tirupati Devasthanams (TTD) applied in 2008, and the Tirupati Laddu was registered as a GI in 2009. A public interest petition against it in the Madras High Court was dismissed in 2010, because a rectification application was the proper remedy. A rectification application then argued that a prasadam is not “goods”, that the registration hurts religious feelings (section 9(d)), and that a single body cannot represent producers.

Decision

On 30 July 2012 the Registry dismissed the rectification application because the applicant was not a “person aggrieved”, and imposed costs of ₹10,000.

Lesson

The religious question (can a divine offering be a GI?) has never been decided on its merits. Locus standi can decide a GI dispute.

slides.part: Chapter 6: The important GI cases
slides.title: Basmati (who is inside the GI area?)
slides.html:
Forum

GI Registry, IPAB and the Madras High Court; and the EU registration process.

Story

APEDA applied in 2008 for a GI for Basmati rice grown in the traditional Basmati area of north India. Madhya Pradesh opposed, because its districts had been left out.

Decision

The IPAB ordered registration in APEDA’s favour on 5 February 2016, without Madhya Pradesh. On 27 February 2020 a Division Bench of the Madras High Court dismissed Madhya Pradesh’s challenge. A further appeal was taken to the Supreme Court; its outcome could not be confirmed.

Abroad

India applied for EU protection (as a PGI) in 2018. Pakistan opposed and filed its own application in 2023, which the EU published in 2024. As of late 2025, the dispute was reported as unresolved.

Lesson

The boundaries of the GI area decide who benefits. GIs can cross national borders and become political.

slides.part: Chapter 6: The important GI cases
slides.title: Prada and the Kolhapuri Chappal (2025)
slides.html:
Court

Bombay High Court, 16 July 2025.

Story

At Milan Fashion Week on 22 June 2025, Prada showed sandals that looked very like Kolhapuri chappals, without naming them. Kolhapuri Chappal has been a GI since 2019, held by LIDCOM and LIDKAR for districts of Maharashtra and Karnataka. After public criticism, Prada admitted the sandals were inspired by traditional Indian handmade footwear. A group of Pune lawyers then filed a public interest petition.

Decision

The Bombay High Court dismissed the PIL. It held that GI rights are statutory and proprietary, that only the registered proprietor or authorised users can enforce them, and that infringement cannot be decided in a PIL. The proprietors remained free to sue.

Later

In December 2025, Prada signed an agreement with LIDCOM and LIDKAR for a project of Kolhapuri inspired footwear made in India.

Lesson

A GI protects the name used on goods, not the design or shape. Only proprietors and authorised users can sue. Indian GI law does not reach a fashion show abroad unless goods are sold in India under the name.

slides.part: Chapter 7: GI protection in the European Union
slides.title: Overview
slides.html:
In simple words

The EU has the world’s most developed GI system. It uses different labels for different strengths of link, registers names centrally for all member states, and insists on inspections.

slides.part: Chapter 7: GI protection in the European Union
slides.title: 7.1 The labels
slides.html:
LabelLink with the placeWhere production happensProductsExample
PDO (Protected Designation of Origin)Quality or characteristics essentially or exclusively due to the particular environment, natural and humanAll steps of production, processing and preparation in the areaFood, agricultural products, wineKalamata olive oil, Roquefort, Shetland Lamb
PGI (Protected Geographical Indication)A given quality, reputation or other characteristic essentially attributable to the originAt least one step in the areaFood, agricultural products, wine; and since 1 December 2025, craft and industrial productsWestfälischer Knochenschinken, Scotch Beef, Darjeeling

TSG (Traditional Speciality Guaranteed)No link with a place; it protects a traditional recipe or methodAnywhereFoodNot a GI at all

Labels: the slides say the EU logo is compulsory for PDO and PGI food and agricultural products, optional for wine (noted in the margin of your notes), and optional for spirit drinks.

Your notes vs the law

Your notes say GIs were initially granted as “agriculture: PDO; wines, spirits: GI; food: PGI”. That mapping is not correct. PDO and PGI both cover food, agricultural products and wine; the plain “GI” label is for spirit drinks.

The handwritten line “In EU, GI is only for agricultural product, wine and spirit drinks” was true until 2025. Since 1 December 2025, Regulation (EU) 2023/2411 protects craft and industrial products (such as glass, cutlery, textiles and handlooms) across the EU, through the EU Intellectual Property Office (EUIPO). That is what “recently handlooms, etc added” in your notes refers to.

Your notes write TSG as “Traditional System Gurantee”. The correct name is Traditional Speciality Guaranteed, and your note is right that it is not a GI.

slides.part: Chapter 7: GI protection in the European Union
slides.title: 7.2 PDO and PGI explained through the class examples
slides.html:
Kalamata olive oil (PDO). Made entirely in the Kalamata region of Greece from local olive varieties. Everything happens in the area, so it is a PDO.

Westfälischer Knochenschinken (PGI). A ham made in Westphalia, Germany, using age old techniques, but the meat need not come from animals born and raised there (your note: “meat originates anywhere though”). One key step in the area is enough for a PGI.

Roquefort (PDO). A blue cheese made from raw, whole milk of Lacaune sheep, cultured with the mould Penicillium roqueforti, and ripened for at least 14 days in the natural caves of Mount Combalou at Roquefort sur Soulzon in southern France. The caves stay cool and humid and are naturally ventilated through cracks in the rock called fleurines. Roquefort was the first French cheese to get appellation protection, in 1925.

Your notes vs the law

Your notes describe Roquefort as made in the “anaerobic conditions of caves”. That is not accurate. The mould needs air, and the caves are famous for their natural airflow through the fleurines. Write “cool, humid and naturally ventilated caves” instead.

Irish Whiskey (spirit GI). Distilled and matured in Ireland, although the raw materials do not all come from Ireland. (The slide says it has been made in Ireland since the 6th century; that is a traditional claim that was not verified.)

slides.part: Chapter 7: GI protection in the European Union
slides.title: 7.3 PDO versus PGI: Shetland Lamb and Scotch Beef
slides.html:
PointShetland Lamb (PDO)Scotch Beef (PGI)
AreaConfined to the Shetland IslandsNot precisely defined: most of Scotland, including the mainland, the islands off the west coast, Orkney and Shetland
Rearing ruleAnimals reared for their entire lives, slaughtered and dressed in the areaThe same rule
Why the label differsIts quality is essentially due to the particular environment of the islandsThe link is with the quality and reputation of Scottish beef in general

So both products follow the same rearing rule. The difference lies in how strong and how specific the link with the place is.

Your notes vs the law

One slide says “Shetland Lamb is a PGI” and then “registered as a PDO”. The correct position is PDO: the UK government’s register of protected food names lists Shetland Lamb as a Protected Designation of Origin.

slides.part: Chapter 7: GI protection in the European Union
slides.title: 7.5 National laws for crafts before 2025
slides.html:
Before the new EU law, some member states protected craft GIs under their own national laws (slide):

  • Germany: cutlery, scissors, knives and razor blades from Solingen, under the “Solingen Decree” of 16 December 1994.
  • Italy: “Vetro Artistico Murano” (Murano glass), under a regional law of 2001 that gave glass makers on the island a collective right.

Your notes vs the law

Your notes say “Greece has allowed cutlery to be a GI product”. The slide’s cutlery example is Germany (Solingen), so this looks like a mix up. Your notes also mention “Swiss mechanical watches”; Switzerland is not an EU member, and it protects “Swiss made” watches under its own national law.

slides.part: Chapter 7: GI protection in the European Union
slides.title: 7.6 Handicrafts and single producers
slides.html: Under Regulation 510/2006, a limited number of handicrafts made from agricultural products were covered, for example the essential oil Bergamotto di Reggio Calabria (PDO). Your notes add an exception: even a single person producing a certain handicraft can file, and the GI then relates to that person’s village or area. EU law does allow a single producer to apply in exceptional cases, typically where that producer is the only one in the area. Indian law has no such exception.

slides.part: Chapter 7: GI protection in the European Union
slides.title: 7.7 How a GI is registered in the EU
slides.html:
The producer group writes a detailed product specification

↓

Application to the national authority of the member state

↓

National scrutiny and a national opposition stage

↓

The national decision is made public, and the application goes to the European Commission

↓

The Commission examines the application and can reject it if it does not meet EU law

↓

Publication in the Official Journal of the EU

↓

Opposition within 3 months; if there is an opposition, the parties hold consultations

↓

Registration (or rejection)

Your notes vs the law

The slide shows a “6 month opposition period”. That was the rule under the old Regulation 510/2006. Under the current law, the opposition period is 3 months.

Applications from outside the EU (third countries). A non EU group can apply to the Commission. The slides list four items: the applicant’s name and address, the product specification, a single document summarising it, and proof that the name is protected in its home country (compare TRIPS Article 24.9).

Indian examples. Darjeeling was registered as a PGI in the EU by Regulation (EU) No 1050/2011 of 20 October 2011, the first Indian product protected in this way, after objections from Germany, France, Italy, Austria and the UK. India’s application for Basmati, filed in 2018, is still contested by Pakistan.

slides.part: Chapter 7: GI protection in the European Union
slides.title: 7.8 Quality control and sustainability
slides.html:
In the EU, controls are a precondition of registration: the application must name the body that will check compliance with the product specification, and official controls continue after registration.

Your notes say the EU has a sustainability rule under which the applicant “has to show” sustainability (environmental, social and economic) when filing.

Your notes vs the law

Under Regulation 2024/1143, producer groups may agree on a voluntary basis to sustainability practices that go beyond what the law requires, and these can be written into the product specification. It is voluntary, not a compulsory filing requirement.

slides.part: Chapter 7: GI protection in the European Union
slides.title: 7.9 Numbers from the slides
slides.html: The slides say the EU has over 3,840 GIs (food 1,838; wine 1,730; spirits 272), worth about €75 billion, or 7% of EU food and drink sales, with exports of about €17 billion. These figures come from an EU study published in 2020 using 2017 data. The current numbers are higher, but the latest count was not verified.

slides.part: Chapter 8: GI protection in the United States
slides.title: Overview
slides.html:
In simple words

The US has no separate GI law. It protects GIs through its trade mark system, mainly as certification marks.

Your notes explain why: the US felt that a separate GI law would be an extra burden and that its trade mark system could already protect GIs. TRIPS allows this, because it sets minimum standards but leaves each country free to choose the method.

The US uses three tools:

  • Certification marks: the owner certifies that goods come from the region and meet its standards. Darjeeling tea is protected this way in the US.
  • Collective marks: used by the members of a group or association.
  • Ordinary trade marks, where a geographical name has come to identify one business.

The key rule: first in time, first in right. The earlier right wins. This leads to the issue noted in class: if an Indian GI owner applies for a US certification mark, but someone already owns a US trade mark for the same name, the application will be refused. The class example was Kashmiri Kesar (Kashmir saffron, an Indian GI). No real US case about it could be found, so treat it as a classroom hypothetical that illustrates the risk.

For wine names, the US also relies on its labelling rules, as the semi generic names system shows (Chapter 4).

slides.part: Chapter 9: GI exam guide
slides.title: 9.1 Twelve things you must know
slides.html:
• The four ingredients of the definition in section 2(1)(e): indication, goods, link, local activity.
  • The difference between an indication of source, a GI and an appellation of origin (the three circles).
  • GI versus trade mark: a community right, goods only, and it cannot be licensed (section 24).
  • The four treaties in order, and that India is bound only by Paris and TRIPS.
  • TRIPS Articles 22, 23 and 24, and the two level problem.
  • Who can apply (section 11) and who counts as a producer (section 2(1)(k)).
  • Part A (proprietor) and Part B (authorised users).
  • The seven bars in section 9.
  • The registration steps, the 3 month opposition period and the 10 year renewable term.
  • The three types of infringement in section 22(1), and that the extra protection in section 22(3) applies only to notified goods (so far, only wines and spirits).
  • The five year limit in section 26(4), illustrated by Tea Board v ITC.
  • The EU labels (PDO, PGI, spirit GI) and the US trade mark approach.

slides.part: Chapter 9: GI exam guide
slides.title: 9.2 Common mistakes to avoid
slides.html:
• Saying a GI can cover services. It cannot (Tea Board v ITC).
  • Saying a GI can be licensed or sold. It cannot (section 24).
  • Applying section 22(3) to “Kolhapuri style” goods without noting that the goods must first be notified.
  • Treating the five year limit as starting afresh every day the use continues. Tea Board v ITC rejected that argument.
  • Writing that the EU opposition period is 6 months. It is now 3 months.
  • Calling TSG a GI.
  • Saying India is a member of the Lisbon Agreement. It is not.
  • Writing “Scotch whiskey”. Scotch is spelt whisky; “whiskey” is the Irish and American spelling, as in Irish Whiskey.

slides.part: Chapter 9: GI exam guide
slides.title: 9.3 How to answer a GI problem question
slides.html:
• Issue: state the legal question in one line.
  • Is it a GI? Apply the four ingredients of section 2(1)(e) and the bars in section 9.
  • Is it registered, and who is suing? Only the registered proprietor or authorised users can sue for infringement (section 21). If the GI is not registered, consider passing off (section 20(2)).
  • Is there infringement? Apply section 22(1)(a), (b) or (c), and check whether the goods are notified for section 22(3).
  • Defences: exhaustion (section 22(4)), a prior good faith trade mark (section 26(1)), a common name (section 26(2)), own name (section 26(3)) and the five year limit (section 26(4)).
  • Remedies and conclusion: injunction, damages or profits, delivery up, and criminal liability where there is falsification. Then give a reasoned conclusion.

slides.part: Chapter 9: GI exam guide
slides.title: 9.4 Practice problems with short answers
slides.html:
Practice problem

Problem 1. A café in Kolkata opened in 2019 under the name “Darjeeling Tea Bar”. The Tea Board found out in 2020 but sued only in 2026. Will it succeed?

Suggested answer. (1) The GI covers tea, which is goods; a café is a service, so section 22(1) fits poorly (Tea Board v ITC). (2) If the café registered or used “Darjeeling Tea Bar” as a trade mark, section 26(4) bars action five years after the Tea Board knew, that is from 2025, so a suit in 2026 is too late unless the café acted in bad faith. (3) Passing off may still be argued, but the Tea Board must prove that customers were deceived. Conclusion: the claim is weak.

Practice problem

Problem 2. A mill in Surat sells sarees labelled “Banarasi type silk saree, made in Surat”. Does this infringe the Banarasi GI?

Suggested answer. (1) Section 22(3), which catches words like “type” even when the true origin is shown, applies only to notified goods, and silk sarees are not notified (only wines and spirits are). (2) Under section 22(1)(a), the label states the true origin, so it is harder to prove that buyers are misled. (3) Under section 22(1)(b), the proprietor can argue unfair competition: using “Banarasi” to borrow its reputation is contrary to honest practices and misleads about the nature of the goods. (4) Conclusion: there is an arguable case under section 22(1)(b), and the problem shows why India’s failure to notify goods other than wines and spirits matters.

Practice problem

Problem 3. A temple trust registers its prasadam as a GI. A devotee wants the registration cancelled. Advise.

Suggested answer. (1) Grounds: the bars on hurting religious feelings (section 9(d)) and on matter a court would not protect (section 9(e)); whether a prasadam is “goods” under section 2(1)(f); and whether a single trust can represent producers under section 11. (2) Procedure: rectification under section 27, before the Registrar or the High Court. (3) The main hurdle is locus: the devotee must be a “person aggrieved”, which is where the Tirupati Laddu challenge failed. (4) Conclusion: there are arguable grounds on the merits, but the case may fail at the threshold.
