slides.part: Revision: Geographical Indications on one page
slides.title: Geographical Indications on one page
slides.html:
• Idea: a GI is a name or sign showing that goods come from a place and owe their quality, reputation or characteristic to it (product place linkage).
  • Three circles: indication of source (where made) contains GI (quality link) contains appellation of origin (strictest link).
  • Definition, section 2(1)(e): indication, goods, link, local activity. A non place name such as Basmati can qualify.
  • Versus trade mark: community right, goods only, cannot be sold or licensed (section 24).
  • Treaties: Paris 1883 (India is a member), Madrid 1891 and Lisbon 1958 (India is not), TRIPS 1994 (binding). TRIPS Art. 22 gives basic protection, Art. 23 extra protection for wines and spirits, Art. 24 exceptions.
  • Grandfathering: TRIPS 24.4 (use for 10 years before 15 April 1994, or in good faith before it), 24.5 (old trade marks), and the 2006 US and EU wine deal (COLA before 10 March 2006; same brand and fanciful name).
  • Indian Act: Act 48 of 1999, in force 15 September 2003; Registry at Chennai; Darjeeling Tea was the first GI.
  • Applicant: an association, organisation or authority representing producers (section 11); Part A proprietor, Part B authorised users.
  • Bars (section 9): deceptive, illegal, obscene, religious hurt, not protectable in a court, generic or dead at home, literally true but misleading.
  • Process: examination, advertisement, opposition within 3 months (plus 1), registration; 10 years, renewable forever.
  • Infringement (section 22): misleading use, unfair competition, literally true but misleading; extra protection only for notified goods (so far wines and spirits); resale of genuine goods allowed unless impaired.
  • Trade marks (sections 25, 26): misleading trade marks refused; older good faith marks saved; common names before 1 January 1995 saved; five year limit in section 26(4).
  • Remedies: injunction, damages or profits, delivery up; falsifying a GI is punished with 6 months to 3 years and a fine of ₹50,000 to ₹2 lakh. Appeals now go to the High Court.
  • Key cases: Tea Board v ITC (time bar, goods not services, no confusion); Golden Bottling (passing off); Champagne v Chinar Agro (foreign GI); Bikaji (place of making); Toda (representation); Tirupati Laddu (locus); Basmati (area); Prada Kolhapuri (only proprietors can sue; name, not design).
  • EU: PDO (strongest), PGI (one step), spirit GI; TSG is not a GI; crafts covered since 1 December 2025; opposition 3 months; controls compulsory; sustainability voluntary.
  • US: trade mark system (certification and collective marks); first in time, first in right.

slides.part: Chapter 10: What is a chip and what is a layout design?
slides.title: Overview
slides.html:
A chip, or integrated circuit (IC), is a tiny piece of silicon that holds millions or even billions of transistors (tiny electronic switches), together with other elements such as resistors and capacitors, and the metal wires that connect them. Everything is built into the material itself, which is why it is called “integrated”.

Chips are made layer by layer. For each layer, a mask, which works like a stencil, decides which parts of the silicon wafer are exposed and which are covered during that step. Many masks used one after another build up a three dimensional structure.

Each layer is printed through its own mask (a stencil). The full 3D arrangement of all layers = the layout design (topography).

  1. Metal wiring connecting the parts
  2. Insulating layer
  3. Transistors formed in the silicon
  4. Silicon base (wafer)

A simplified picture. Real chips have many more layers.

The three dimensional arrangement of all these elements and their connections is the layout design, also called the topography. In the US it is called a mask work. Your notes describe it as the “3D disposition of the special patterns, which defines the structure of circuit”.

In simple words

Think of a building with many floors. The layout design is the complete set of floor plans showing where every room, wire and staircase goes on every floor. The chip is the finished building.

slides.part: Chapter 10: What is a chip and what is a layout design?
slides.title: 10.1 Moore’s Law
slides.html:
Your notes vs the law

Your notes say Moore’s Law means the “doubling of no. of chips, halving the size of computers”. The correct version: Gordon Moore, one of the founders of Intel, observed in 1965 that the number of components (transistors) on a single chip was doubling about every year, and in 1975 he revised this to about every two years. That is why chips keep getting more powerful and cheaper. It is about the transistors on a chip, not the number of chips.

slides.part: Chapter 10: What is a chip and what is a layout design?
slides.title: 10.2 Why chip designs need protection
slides.html:
• Designing a chip is slow and expensive. The slides say developing an IC can involve around 500 process steps, take more than two years and draw on the know how of thousands of engineers.
  • Copying is quick and cheap. A copier can strip a chip layer by layer, photograph each layer, and make masks from the photographs. Your notes call this chip piracy: years of research (“15 to 20 years” in your notes, a classroom figure) copied and sold at low prices.
  • Chips are strategic. Countries now treat chip design and manufacturing as matters of national security (Chapter 11).

slides.part: Chapter 11: Background: history and the Chip War
slides.title: Overview
slides.html: This chapter is background that was taught in class. It is useful for introductions and context, but it is not law.

slides.part: Chapter 11: Background: history and the Chip War
slides.title: 11.1 A short history
slides.html:
• 1947: Bell Labs announced the first successful transistor. John Bardeen, Walter Brattain and William Shockley later won the Nobel Prize for it.
  • 1958 and 1959: Jack Kilby at Texas Instruments and Robert Noyce at Fairchild Semiconductor invented the integrated circuit independently. The two companies got separate patents, and these became the basic patent coverage for ICs and helped launch the chip business of Silicon Valley.
  • Japan: from the 1950s Japan built its own semiconductor industry. The Sony TR55 was the first transistor radio made in Japan, NEC developed its first IC around 1960, and Hayakawa Electric (the predecessor of Sharp) sold the world’s first all transistor desktop calculator in 1964.
  • 1970s onward: Texas Instruments and Intel both claimed the first microprocessor (1970 to 1971). Japanese firms became strong rivals. Computer design tools allowed chip design to be separated from manufacturing, and Asia became the centre of mass production.

Your notes vs the law

The slide writes “Jak Kilby”; the correct name is Jack Kilby. The slide also credits Kilby with linking components using aluminium lines on top of a protective oxide layer; that description fits Noyce’s planar design at Fairchild better than Kilby’s first device. The other details on the history slide (Volta in 1782, Bose’s patent, De Forest, Lilienfeld) are background only and were not separately verified.

slides.part: Chapter 11: Background: history and the Chip War
slides.title: 11.2 The Chip War
slides.html:
• US CHIPS and Science Act (August 2022): large subsidies to boost chip manufacturing in the US, reduce dependence on imports and protect supply chains (your notes: “to boost domestic semiconductor production, int’l competition”).
  • Export controls (October 2022): limits on exporting advanced chips and chipmaking equipment to China, aimed at chips made at about 14 or 16 nanometres and below.
  • “Small yard, high fence”: protect a small set of critical technologies very strongly, rather than restricting all trade.
  • The EU approach: “de risking and diversifying” rather than “decoupling” from China.
  • “Chip 4 Alliance”: a US proposal with Japan, South Korea and Taiwan to make East Asia’s chip supply chain more secure.
  • Taiwan’s dominance: a 2021 report by the Semiconductor Industry Association and Boston Consulting Group found that 92% of the world’s most advanced chipmaking capacity (below 10 nanometres) was in Taiwan, and the rest in South Korea.
  • Book: “Chip War” by Chris Miller (2022), recommended in class.

Why this matters for the law: chip layout designs are now strategic assets, so protecting them is part of both IP law and trade policy.

slides.part: Chapter 12: Why ordinary IP laws did not fit
slides.title: Overview
slides.html:
In simple words

Chip layouts fell into a gap. They were too ordinary for patents, too functional for copyright, and too easy to copy for trade secrets. So countries created a new, special right.

Existing rightWhy it did not work for chip layouts
PatentA patent needs a new invention with an inventive step. Most new layouts are clever arrangements of known circuit elements, and your notes say “patent cannot protect mere rearrangement”. In India, section 3(f) of the Patents Act, 1970 excludes the mere arrangement or rearrangement of known devices. Patents are also slow and costly compared with the short life of a chip.
CopyrightCopyright protects expression, not function, and your notes say “copyright cannot protect functional aspects”. A layout is largely dictated by its electronic function. The US Copyright Office refused to register chip patterns because no separate artistic features were shown.
Trade secretOnce a chip is sold, anyone can open it up and study it, so secrecy is lost.

slides.part: Chapter 12: Why ordinary IP laws did not fit
slides.title: 12.1 Attempts to stretch copyright
slides.html:
H.R. 1007 (US, 1979) proposed adding the masks used to imprint chip patterns, and the patterns themselves, to copyright as pictorial, graphic and sculptural works. It was not adopted. The slides add that the copyright route was seen as unworkable because the Universal Copyright Convention mainly concerned works of applied art, and that later drafts which created a separate category of rights also failed to fit into the copyright statute.

L.B. (Plastics) Ltd v Swish Products Ltd (House of Lords, UK, 1979). The slide says this case held that mask works are protectable under copyright. That overstates it. The case was about plastic drawer components: the House of Lords held that copying a three dimensional object can infringe the copyright in its technical drawings. Commentators then argued that, by the same logic, a chip could be a “copy” of its design drawings. The case itself said nothing about chips.

NEC v Intel (United States)

Story

NEC’s V20 and V30 chips were compatible with Intel’s famous 8086 and 8088 processors. The dispute was about microcode, the internal software instructions inside a chip.

What happened

NEC went to court first, asking for a declaration that it did not infringe, and Intel claimed infringement. In September 1986 Judge Ingram ruled that microcode can be protected by copyright; he later withdrew from the case because he held a small amount of Intel stock. In February 1989 Judge Gray held that microcode is copyrightable, but that Intel had lost copyright in some of it by distributing chips without a copyright notice, and that NEC’s microcode, written independently in a “clean room”, did not infringe.

Lesson

The case was about chip software, not the layout, so it showed that copyright could not solve the layout piracy problem.

Your notes vs the law

The slide says “NEC was held to have copied” Intel’s chips and that “Intel sued NEC” in 1986. Both are inaccurate: NEC started the case, and in the end NEC was found not to infringe.

slides.part: Chapter 12: Why ordinary IP laws did not fit
slides.title: 12.2 The answer: a special (sui generis) right
slides.html:
Your notes say the US Semiconductor Chip Protection Act, 1984 (SCPA) “created a new kind of legislation (patent + copyright + competition)”. It borrowed:

  • from copyright: the originality test and protection against copying;
  • from patent law: registration and a short, fixed term;
  • from competition law: the freedom to reverse engineer and build better, competing chips.

slides.part: Chapter 13: How the world responded
slides.title: 13.1 United States: the SCPA, 1984
slides.html:
• It protects mask works fixed in semiconductor chip products, if they are original and not staple, commonplace or familiar in the industry.
  • Protection lasts 10 years.
  • The owner must apply for registration with the US Copyright Office within 2 years of first commercial exploitation, or protection ends.
  • Reverse engineering is allowed (section 906(a)): a person may copy a mask work solely to teach, analyse or evaluate its concepts or techniques, and may then use the results in their own original mask work. Your notes record this exactly.
  • Innocent buyers of infringing chips are protected until they receive notice, after which they pay a reasonable royalty.
  • Reciprocity: foreign chips were protected only if the foreign country protected US chips. This pushed other countries to pass similar laws quickly.

slides.part: Chapter 13: How the world responded
slides.title: 13.2 Japan, 1985
slides.html: Japan passed a similar law in 1985 (the slides give the date as 31 May 1985).

slides.part: Chapter 13: How the world responded
slides.title: 13.3 European Community: Directive 87/54/EEC of 16 December 1986
slides.html:
• It protects the topography, not the chip itself (your notes): “the three dimensional pattern of the layers of which a semiconductor product is composed”.
  • A topography is protected if it is the result of its creator’s own intellectual effort and is not commonplace in the semiconductor industry (Article 2(2)).
  • The right holder must be a national of a member state or start commercial exploitation in the Community; otherwise protection depends on special arrangements (Article 3).
  • The holder has the exclusive right to authorise or prohibit reproduction and commercial exploitation (Article 5).
  • Reverse engineering for analysis and teaching is allowed, and protection lasts about 10 years.

slides.part: Chapter 13: How the world responded
slides.title: 13.4 The IPIC (Washington) Treaty, 1989
slides.html:
Because the US insisted on reciprocity, countries wanted common international minimum standards. WIPO held a diplomatic conference in Washington, which adopted the Treaty on Intellectual Property in Respect of Integrated Circuits on 26 May 1989.

  • Definitions (Article 2): an integrated circuit is a product, in final or intermediate form, in which the elements (at least one of them active) and some or all of the interconnections are integrally formed in or on a piece of material, and which is meant to perform an electronic function. A layout design is the three dimensional disposition of those elements and interconnections.
  • Originality (Article 3): the design must be the result of its creator’s own intellectual effort and not commonplace among layout designers and chip makers when it was created. A combination of commonplace elements is protected if the combination, taken as a whole, is original.
  • Rights (Article 6): reproducing the design, and importing, selling or distributing it commercially, need the owner’s permission.
  • Term (Article 8): at least 8 years.
  • Compulsory licences (Article 6(3)): allowed in certain cases.

Why it failed: the US and Japan objected, mainly to the short 8 year term and the wide compulsory licensing rules. The treaty has never entered into force; only Bosnia and Herzegovina, Egypt and Saint Lucia have ratified or acceded to it. India signed it but has not ratified it.

Your notes vs the law

The slide calls it the “Treaty on the Protection of Intellectual Property in Respect of Integrated Circuits”. The official name does not include “the Protection of”: it is the Treaty on Intellectual Property in Respect of Integrated Circuits.

slides.part: Chapter 13: How the world responded
slides.title: 13.5 TRIPS Articles 35 to 38: the binding rules
slides.html:
TRIPS rescued the IPIC Treaty by making most of it binding through the WTO, with some changes.

  • Article 35: members must protect layout designs according to IPIC Articles 2 to 7 (but not Article 6(3) on compulsory licences), Article 12 and Article 16(3), plus the TRIPS rules below.
  • Article 36 (scope): importing, selling or distributing for commercial purposes a protected layout design, a chip containing it, or an article containing such a chip (for example, a phone) is unlawful without permission, as long as the article still contains the unlawfully copied design.
  • Article 37(1) (innocent buyers): a person who did not know, and had no reasonable ground to know, that a chip contained a pirated design is not liable. After receiving notice, they may still sell the stock they already have or have ordered, but must pay the owner a reasonable royalty.
  • Article 37(2) (compulsory licences): a non voluntary licence, or use by the government, is allowed only under the strict patent conditions in Article 31(a) to (k).
  • Article 38 (term): where registration is required, protection must last at least 10 years from filing or from first commercial exploitation anywhere in the world; where no registration is required, at least 10 years from first commercial exploitation. A member may also provide that protection ends 15 years after the design was created.

Your notes vs the law

Your notes say “Max 15 years”. To be precise, TRIPS sets a minimum of 10 years, and the 15 year limit is only an option (Article 38(3)) that a country may adopt. It is not a compulsory maximum.

slides.part: Chapter 14: India’s Semiconductor Integrated Circuits Layout Design Act, 2000
slides.title: Overview
slides.html:
In simple words

India protects registered chip layout designs that are original and distinctive, for 10 years. The owner gets the exclusive right to use the design, but research, teaching and reverse engineering are still allowed.

slides.part: Chapter 14: India’s Semiconductor Integrated Circuits Layout Design Act, 2000
slides.title: 14.1 Basic facts
slides.html:
• Act No. 37 of 2000, which received the President’s assent on 4 September 2000. Your notes call it the SICLD Act, 2000.
  • It was passed because India, having ratified TRIPS, had to give effect to Section 6 of Part II of TRIPS (layout designs).
  • It has its own Registrar of Semiconductor Integrated Circuits Layout Design and its own Registry, separate from the GI Registry. The Semiconductor Integrated Circuits Layout Design Rules, 2001 lay down the forms and fees.
  • In practice it is hardly used. Your notes say “only 2 layout designs registered so far”. Exact figures differ between sources: a 2026 analysis by the law firm S.S. Rana, based on official annual reports, says only about 31 applications have ever been filed, with a handful of registrations in recent years (3 in 2022 to 2023, 2 in 2023 to 2024 and none in 2024 to 2025). The point is the same: the law is almost never used. No reported court decision under the Act was found.

slides.part: Chapter 14: India’s Semiconductor Integrated Circuits Layout Design Act, 2000
slides.title: 14.2 What the Act protects
slides.html:
Two definitions were taught:

  • Semiconductor integrated circuit (section 2(r)): a product with transistors and other circuit elements that are inseparably formed on a semiconductor material or an insulating material, or inside the semiconductor material, and that is designed to perform an electronic circuitry function.
  • Layout design (section 2(h)): a layout of transistors and other circuit elements, including the lead wires connecting them, expressed in any manner in a semiconductor integrated circuit.

Protection is only for registered layout designs; there is no infringement action for an unregistered one (section 16).

slides.part: Chapter 14: India’s Semiconductor Integrated Circuits Layout Design Act, 2000
slides.title: 14.3 When a layout design cannot be registered
slides.html:
Section 7(1) lists four bars. In simple words, a layout design cannot be registered if it is:

  • not original;
  • already commercially exploited in India or in a convention country;
  • not inherently distinctive; or
  • not inherently capable of being distinguished from any other registered layout design.

The two year grace period. A design that has been commercially exploited for not more than two years before the application date is treated as not exploited. So a company can sell its chip for up to two years and still register the design.

Your notes vs the law

Your handwritten list (“not original, not distinctive, incapable of being distinguished”) leaves out the bar on prior commercial exploitation and the two year grace period. Include all four bars and the proviso in your answer.

What “original” means (section 7(2)). Your notes: “result of creator’s own intellectual efforts and not commonly known to the creators working in the industry”. Exactly: the design must result from the creator’s own intellectual effort and must not be commonly known to layout designers and chip makers when it was created. A design made up of commonly known elements can still be original if the combination, taken as a whole, results from the creator’s own effort. This is the same idea as “not commonplace” in the EU Directive and the IPIC Treaty.

How is distinctiveness judged? The Act gives no list. The class slides list practical factors that help show a design is distinctive. Grouped simply:

  • the components used and how they are grouped;
  • the key function the circuit performs (for example, controlling a mobile display, a gaming function or a robot motor);
  • timing: clock rate, read, write or refresh signals, and frequency;
  • the method used for calculations;
  • the interconnections (how the parts interact electrically);
  • power sharing and power lines (the power topology);
  • the number of layers (single, double, triple or more) and the 3D pattern;
  • energy consumption and heat dissipation, if innovative;
  • passive elements, memory and operating temperature;
  • the package (for example dual in line or moulded) and physical details such as device holes, lead pitch, film thickness and materials.

The slide’s final point is the most important: the design must be judged as a whole. Remember that this list is classroom guidance, not part of the Act.

slides.part: Chapter 14: India’s Semiconductor Integrated Circuits Layout Design Act, 2000
slides.title: 14.5 How long protection lasts
slides.html:
Section 15: registration lasts 10 years, counted from the date of filing or the date of first commercial exploitation anywhere in India or in any other country, whichever is earlier. There is no renewal.

In simple words: worked example

Example. A chip using a new design is first sold in Japan in March 2025, and the Indian application is filed in January 2026. First exploitation (March 2025) is earlier than filing, so protection runs until March 2035. The two year grace period is met, because the design had been sold for less than two years before filing.

slides.part: Chapter 14: India’s Semiconductor Integrated Circuits Layout Design Act, 2000
slides.title: 14.6 Rights of the registered owner
slides.html: Section 17: registration gives the registered proprietor the exclusive right to use the layout design and to obtain relief for infringement. The Explanation adds that these rights exist whether or not the design is actually incorporated in an article such as a chip. The registration certificate is prima facie evidence of validity (section 19).

slides.part: Chapter 14: India’s Semiconductor Integrated Circuits Layout Design Act, 2000
slides.title: 14.7 Infringement and the exceptions
slides.html:
A person who is not the registered proprietor or a registered user infringes if they (section 18(1)):

  • reproduce the registered layout design, in whole or in part, by putting it in a chip or in any other way (except a part that is not original); or
  • import, sell or otherwise distribute for commercial purposes the design, a chip containing it, or an article containing such a chip.

The exceptions are what examiners like to ask about:

SituationInfringes?Why
Copying the design for scientific evaluation, analysis, research or teaching (18(2))NoThe research and teaching exception
Studying a registered design and creating a new original design, then using and selling it (18(3))NoReverse engineering that produces something original is allowed (compare SCPA section 906(a))
The original owner using that new design after it is registered by its creator (18(4))YesOnce registered, the new design belongs to its creator, so even the earlier owner cannot use it
Selling chips without knowing they contain a registered design (18(5))No, until noticeThe innocent infringer rule. After notice, the seller may sell stock on hand or already ordered, but must pay a royalty, fixed by negotiation or by the Appellate Board
Buying such chips from the innocent seller (18(6))NoThe buyer gets the same immunity
Dealing with chips sold by or with the consent of the owner, or with written consent (18(7))NoExhaustion and consent
Creating an identical design independently, by one’s own intellect (18(8))NoIndependent creation is not copying

Your notes vs the law

Your notes and the slides cover sub sections (1) to (5). Sub sections (6) to (8) are also in the Act; they are added here because they complete the picture of the defences. The Act provides for an Appellate Board to fix the royalty under section 18(5); secondary sources suggest this Board was never actually set up, but that could not be confirmed.

slides.part: Chapter 14: India’s Semiconductor Integrated Circuits Layout Design Act, 2000
slides.title: 14.9 Why is the Act so rarely used?
slides.html:
These are possible reasons (analysis, not official findings):

  • Chip life cycles are short, and companies move to the next design quickly.
  • Copying a complete modern chip is very hard, so companies rely more on patents, trade secrets and contracts.
  • Many Indian firms are design houses working for foreign clients, who protect their IP abroad.
  • Awareness of the Act and of the separate Registry is low.

With the India Semiconductor Mission and new chip plants being set up in India, the Act may become more relevant in future.

slides.part: Chapter 14: India’s Semiconductor Integrated Circuits Layout Design Act, 2000
slides.title: 14.10 Semiconductor exam guide
slides.html:
Key points to remember:

  • Layout design means the 3D arrangement of a chip’s elements and connections (also called topography, or mask work in the US).
  • Patent and copyright did not fit, so a sui generis right was created; the US SCPA of 1984 was the first.
  • The IPIC Treaty of 1989 never entered into force; TRIPS Articles 35 to 38 made its rules binding.
  • TRIPS term: at least 10 years; the 15 year cap is optional.
  • India: Act 37 of 2000; four bars in section 7 plus the two year grace period; “original” means own effort and not commonly known.
  • Term in India: 10 years from filing or first exploitation, whichever is earlier; no renewal.
  • Section 18: the research and teaching exception, the reverse engineering right, the innocent infringer royalty and independent creation.

Practice problem

Firm X buys a chip whose layout is registered in India, studies it in a university lab, designs an improved and original layout, and sells chips using its own design. Firm Y imports copies of the original chip, not knowing the design is registered. Advise the owner of the registered design.

Suggested answer. (1) The owner has the exclusive rights in section 17. (2) X’s study is protected by section 18(2), and its sale of a new original design by section 18(3), as long as the new design meets section 7(2). (3) Y’s import is prima facie infringement under section 18(1)(b), but under section 18(5) Y is not liable until it receives notice; after notice, it may sell its existing stock but must pay a royalty. (4) Check that the registration is still within the 10 years in section 15. (5) Compare TRIPS Article 37(1). Conclusion: no claim against X; a royalty claim against Y after notice.

slides.part: Revision: Semiconductor layout designs on one page
slides.title: Semiconductor layout designs on one page
slides.html:
• Layout design (topography, mask work): the 3D arrangement of a chip’s elements and connections, built layer by layer through masks.
  • Moore’s Law: transistors on a chip double about every two years (not the number of chips).
  • Why a special law: patents do not cover mere rearrangement; copyright does not cover function; trade secrets are lost once a chip is sold. Hence a sui generis right mixing patent, copyright and competition ideas.
  • US SCPA 1984: mask works, 10 years, registration within 2 years, reverse engineering allowed (section 906(a)), reciprocity.
  • EC Directive 87/54/EEC: protects the topography, not the chip; own effort and not commonplace.
  • IPIC (Washington) Treaty 1989: 8 year term and compulsory licences; opposed by the US and Japan; never in force; India signed only.
  • TRIPS Arts 35 to 38: IPIC rules made binding (except Art. 6(3)); articles containing chips covered; innocent buyers protected with a royalty after notice; at least 10 years, with an optional 15 year cap.
  • India, Act 37 of 2000: four bars in section 7 (not original, already exploited, not distinctive, not distinguishable) with a 2 year grace period; original means own effort and not commonly known; design judged as a whole.
  • Process: advertised within 14 days of acceptance; opposition within 3 months (plus 1); counter statement within 2 months.
  • Term: 10 years from filing or first commercial exploitation, whichever is earlier; no renewal.
  • Rights and infringement: exclusive right to use (section 17); copying or commercial dealing infringes (section 18); exceptions for research and teaching, reverse engineering into a new original design, innocent infringers (royalty after notice), buyers from them, consent and exhaustion, and independent creation.
  • Reality: very few filings and registrations; no reported court decision found.

quiz.concept: Indication of source versus GI
quiz.q: Sundarkot Pens Ltd prints 'Made in Sundarkot' on its ballpoint pens. The pens are ordinary mass-produced pens, no better or worse than pens made anywhere else. Which change in the facts would most clearly turn 'Sundarkot' from a mere indication of source into a geographical indication?
quiz.ok: The pens gain a nib hand-finished in the town by a craft found only there, which buyers prize
no: Every stage of making moves into Sundarkot, though the pens stay no better than any others
The company registers 'Sundarkot' as its trade mark, so that no rival can use the town's name
Sundarkot becomes a famous tourist town, so its name is now widely known across the country
quiz.why: A GI needs a product-place link: some quality, reputation or other characteristic of the goods must be due to the place, whereas an indication of source such as 'Made in India' only says where goods were made. A nib finished in the town by a craft found only there gives the pens a quality owed to local human skill. Moving every stage of production into Sundarkot fails because the pens would still be ordinary, so the name would remain a mere statement of where they were made.

quiz.concept: Reputation-based GI versus appellation
quiz.q: Rangmati, a hill town, has woven shawls for two centuries, and all the weaving still happens there. Tests show the shawls are physically no different from shawls woven elsewhere, but buyers pay a premium because of the town's long reputation for them. How should 'Rangmati shawl' be classified?
quiz.ok: As a GI, since reputation alone can supply the link, but not as an appellation of origin
no: As an appellation of origin, since the whole process of weaving takes place within the town
As an indication of source only, since no physical quality of the shawls comes from the town
As neither, since a manufactured good can be a GI only if its raw material is also local
quiz.why: For a GI, a given quality, reputation or other characteristic must be essentially attributable to the place, so reputation alone can be enough, and for manufactured goods at least one stage of making must happen there. An appellation of origin is stricter: its quality and characteristics must be due exclusively or essentially to the natural and human environment. Rangmati shawls have a place-based reputation and are woven in the town but owe no quality to it, so they are a GI but not an AO; local weaving alone does not make an appellation.

quiz.concept: Legal test for an appellation of origin
quiz.q: Alvera blue cheese gets its flavour and texture from the local pastures and from the cave-ripening skills of Alvera's cheesemakers; only the salt is brought in from outside the area. In a moot, Priya argues that the imported salt by itself rules out treating 'Alvera blue' as an appellation of origin on the Lisbon model. What is the flaw in her argument?
quiz.ok: She treats a memory aid as the legal test, which asks whether quality is due exclusively or essentially to the area
no: There is no flaw; an appellation of origin requires every raw material, process and skill to come from the area
She overlooks that an appellation of origin, like any GI, needs only a reputation that is linked to the area
She overlooks that the Lisbon test looks only at the makers' skill, not at pastures or other natural factors
quiz.why: The class description of an appellation of origin, with all raw materials, process, labour and skill coming from the place, is a good memory aid, and in practice the whole product usually does come from the area. But the legal test in Lisbon Article 2 is whether the quality and characteristics are due exclusively or essentially to the geographical environment, including natural and human factors, so Priya cannot treat one imported input as decisive without asking that question. The 'no flaw' option states the memory aid as if it were the law, which the notes warn against, and the 'skill only' option forgets that natural factors count too.

quiz.concept: Home protection as a precondition abroad
quiz.q: Country X has never passed a GI law, and nothing in its law protects 'Sonagiri rice', its best-known product name. A trader in Country Y, a fellow WTO member, sells rice grown elsewhere as 'Sonagiri rice', and buyers in Y are plainly misled. X's growers ask Y to stop the use under TRIPS. Must Y do so, and why?
quiz.ok: No; TRIPS does not oblige it to protect a GI that is not protected in its home country
no: Yes; buyers in Y are misled, and TRIPS requires every member to stop misleading use of a GI
No; TRIPS protects GIs only for wines and spirits, so a rice name falls outside its scope
No; TRIPS protects only names entered on an international register, which this one is not
quiz.why: Under TRIPS Article 24.9 there is no obligation to protect a GI that is not protected, or has fallen into disuse, in its home country; that is why the notes say India needed its own GI law before it could fight for Darjeeling or Basmati abroad. The basic protection in Article 22.2(a) would normally require Y to provide legal means to stop use that misleads the public, but that duty does not arise for a name its home country leaves unprotected. The wine-only and register options fail because TRIPS also protects other GIs at the basic level, and its protection does not depend on any international register (the talks on one for wine GIs have never finished).

quiz.concept: GI law versus passing off
quiz.q: The Chandravali Weavers' Cooperative has brought five passing off actions in five years against traders selling machine-made cloth as 'Chandravali weave', and each case was slow and costly. A member asks what GI protection would add. Which answer best captures the main advantage?
quiz.ok: A community right, registered once, that every authorised producer may then enforce
no: A right the cooperative could license to mills outside Chandravali in return for royalties
A right covering the weavers' services as well as their cloth, as a trade mark would
A permanent right that never needs renewal, unlike a trade mark that must be renewed
quiz.why: Before GI laws, such names were protected through trade marks, unfair trade practice laws and passing off, but passing off needs proof of reputation, misrepresentation and damage in every single case, which is slow and costly. A special GI law gives a community right that is registered once and can be enforced by every authorised producer. The licensing option fails because a GI cannot be assigned or licensed; GI law also covers goods only, and a registration lasts ten years, renewable without limit.

quiz.concept: Goods ingredient: services excluded
quiz.q: Pallavgiri is famous for a style of herbal massage that local practitioners have refined over generations. Their association applies to register 'Pallavgiri massage' as a GI for the massage itself, arguing that the local herbs and the practitioners' inherited skill give it a character found nowhere else. How should the application fare against the definition, and why?
quiz.ok: It fails, because a massage is a service, and only goods can be registered as GIs
no: It succeeds, because the local herbs and inherited skill supply the link with the place
It succeeds, because a GI, like a trade mark, may be registered for goods or services
It fails, because a place name only describes where something comes from, so it is barred
quiz.why: The four ingredients are an indication, goods, a link with the place and, for manufactured goods, local activity. The goods ingredient covers agricultural, natural and manufactured goods, handicrafts, goods of industry and foodstuff, but not services, so a massage fails at the second step, and a strong link with the place cannot make up for that. The trade mark option borrows the neighbouring regime, since trade marks cover goods and services while GIs cover goods only, and the place-name option gives the right result for the wrong reason: trade mark law refuses place names as merely descriptive, but GI law protects them because the place is the whole point.

quiz.concept: A GI need not be a place name
quiz.q: 'Rasmadhuri' is a traditional sweet made only in three districts of one state, and its texture is credited to the local milk and the cooks' methods. 'Rasmadhuri' is not the name of any country, region or locality. A rival maker opposes GI registration on that ground alone. Is the opposition sound, and why?
quiz.ok: No; a non-place name can be a GI where it relates to a specific area, as Basmati does
no: Yes; a non-place name can be protected only as a trade mark, never as a GI
No; any traditional product name can be a GI, whether or not it relates to an area
Yes; a non-place name can be a GI only where the goods are agricultural, like Basmati
quiz.why: The Explanation to section 2(1)(e) of the GI Act says that a name which is not the name of a country, region or locality can still be a GI if it relates to a specific area; Basmati is the classic example. Rasmadhuri relates to three districts and its qualities are credited to them, so the opposition fails on that ground. The 'any traditional name' option goes too far, because the name must still relate to a specific area, and nothing limits the rule to agricultural goods.

quiz.concept: Local activity for manufactured goods
quiz.q: Velanad chappals owe their reputation to the hand-stitching of artisans in Velanad district. A Pune company hires artisans trained in Velanad and makes chappals in its Pune factory by exactly the same methods. Which change in the facts would let its chappals satisfy the local activity ingredient of the definition?
quiz.ok: The company moves its stitching and finishing to a workshop inside Velanad district
no: The company employs only artisans who were born and raised in Velanad district
The company prints its true Pune address next to the word 'Velanad' on every box
The company pays the Velanad producers' body a yearly fee for consent to use the name
quiz.why: For manufactured goods, the definition requires at least one of the activities of production, processing or preparation to take place in the territory, region or locality, as with Kolhapuri chappals made by artisans in the registered districts. At present none of those activities happens in Velanad, and moving the stitching and finishing there would meet the requirement. Hiring Velanad-born artisans fails because the test looks at where the activity happens, not where the workers come from.

quiz.concept: No licensing of a GI right
quiz.q: The Kanakpur Silk Weavers' Association is the registered proprietor of the 'Kanakpur silk' GI. A Mumbai fashion house offers it a large yearly royalty for a licence to use the name on sarees that will be woven on the fashion house's own looms inside Kanakpur. How should the association be advised?
quiz.ok: No licence can be granted, but a producer in Kanakpur may apply to be an authorised user
no: It may grant the licence, as any trade mark proprietor may license its mark for royalties
It may grant the licence, because the sarees will be woven on looms inside Kanakpur itself
No licence can be granted, and only the association itself may ever use the registered name
quiz.why: A GI is a community right: a producers' body is the registered proprietor and every qualifying producer can become an authorised user, but the right cannot be assigned, transmitted, licensed, pledged or mortgaged (section 24 of the GI Act). A royalty licence is therefore impossible wherever the looms are. The option saying only the association may ever use the name overlooks the authorised user route, which is how a genuine local producer comes to use a GI.

quiz.concept: Descriptive place names versus generic names
quiz.q: Rahul reads the class table row saying that under GI law 'mostly generic names with location name were protected'. He concludes that bakers in the town of Morvel can register 'Morvel bun' as a GI, although across the country 'Morvel bun' is now just the everyday name for any sweet glazed bun, wherever it is baked. What is the flaw in his reasoning?
quiz.ok: The row means names like Darjeeling Tea; a name that no longer tells buyers the origin is generic and barred
no: There is no flaw; any name joining a place to a product word can be a GI if bakers from that place apply
The flaw is that GI law, like trade mark law, refuses any name that joins a place to a product word
The flaw is that a generic name can still be protected, but only as a certification mark, not a GI
quiz.why: The confusing row means that a GI usually joins a place name to the ordinary name of the product, such as Darjeeling + Tea, which trade mark law treats as merely descriptive but GI law protects. A name that has truly become generic, a common word for a type of product that no longer tells you where it comes from, cannot be registered under either law (section 9(f) of the GI Act), as with 'French fries'. 'Morvel bun' now means any glazed bun wherever it is baked, so Rahul's claim fails; the certification mark option is wrong because trade mark law refuses generic names too.

quiz.concept: Who may own a certification mark
quiz.q: Hillcrest Traders, one of the biggest buyers and sellers of Meghavan tea, applies under Indian trade mark law for a certification mark of its own, certifying that tea comes from Meghavan. It promises to certify rival sellers' tea fairly. What is the main obstacle to the application?
quiz.ok: Such a mark cannot be registered in the name of a person who trades in the goods it certifies
no: Such a mark may certify the quality or standard of goods, but never their geographical origin
Such a mark can be granted only after the company becomes an authorised user of a Meghavan GI
Such a mark is an individual right, so it cannot be used to certify other sellers' tea at all
quiz.why: A certification mark is a trade mark certifying that goods meet a standard, such as their origin or quality; its owner certifies other people's goods, and under Indian trade mark law it cannot be registered in the name of someone who trades in those goods. Hillcrest buys and sells Meghavan tea, so it is barred however fairly it promises to act; the Tea Board's Darjeeling certification marks are an example of such marks. The option saying these marks cannot certify origin is wrong, because origin is one of the standards a certification mark can certify.

quiz.concept: Parmesan case: evocation, not genericness
quiz.q: A German dairy sells cheese in the EU as 'Parmesan, made in Germany'; the cheese is not made to the Parmigiano Reggiano specification. Its lawyer argues that because the European Commission lost the Parmesan case against Germany, the dairy may use 'Parmesan' freely. Is the argument sound, and why?
quiz.ok: No; the Commission lost only on a procedural point, and 'Parmesan' was held to evoke the protected name
no: Yes; the Commission lost because the Court found that 'Parmesan' had become a generic name for hard cheese
Yes; the Court held that a label showing the true German origin removes any risk of evoking the Italian name
No; the Court found 'Parmesan' generic only inside Germany, so the dairy may not sell it in other EU states
quiz.why: In European Commission v Germany (2008) the Court of Justice held that 'Parmesan' evokes the protected name 'Parmigiano Reggiano', so it may not be used for cheese not made to that specification even if the true origin is shown, and Germany could not prove that the name had become generic. The Commission lost only on a procedural point: it had not proved that Germany failed to enforce the protection. The lawyer reads that procedural loss as a ruling on the name, which it was not.

quiz.concept: Parma ham: slicing within the region
quiz.q: A supermarket buys whole, genuine Parma hams from the region, slices and packs them in its own plant abroad, and sells the packs as 'Parma ham'. Its lawyer argues that since the ham is genuine and comes from the region, a rule about where it is sliced and packed cannot form part of the name's protection. On the approach the Court took in the Parma ham case, is the argument sound, and why?
quiz.ok: No; even slicing and packing may be required to happen in the region, to protect quality and reputation
no: Yes; a GI governs where the product is made, so steps taken after production fall outside its reach
Yes, unless the producers prove that the sliced packs are of poorer quality than those sliced in Italy
No; the producers own the name, so they may attach any condition they like to later sales of the ham
quiz.why: In Consorzio del Prosciutto di Parma v Asda (2003) the Court accepted that even the slicing and packaging of Parma ham may be required to happen in the region, to protect its quality and reputation. So the fact that the ham itself is genuine does not put slicing and packing outside the name's protection, and the 'production only' option fails. The 'any condition' option goes too far, because the requirement was accepted as a way to protect quality and reputation, not because producers may impose whatever terms they like; nor did the Court ask for proof that particular packs were worse.

quiz.concept: Paris remedies depend on national law
quiz.q: Country Z belongs to the Paris Convention, but its law gives no power to seize falsely labelled goods or to bar their import. Carpets falsely labelled as made in Tarangi arrive, and Tarangi's producers demand seizure. Z offers them only the civil action that its own law provides. Is Z in breach of the Paris Convention, and why?
quiz.ok: No; where its law allows no seizure, Paris lets it rely on the other remedies its own law gives
no: Yes; Paris makes seizure on importation compulsory for every member, whatever its own law says
No; Paris covers only appellations of origin that have been registered at WIPO's International Bureau
Yes; Paris obliges a member to adopt the Madrid rule on seizure once false goods reach its border
quiz.why: Paris Article 10 applies the Article 9 seizure rule to goods with a false indication of source, but if a country's law does not allow seizure on importation, it may use the other actions and remedies its own law provides. That is why the class listed, as a limitation, that sanctions then depend entirely on national law. Z's civil action therefore satisfies Paris; the WIPO registration option describes the Lisbon system, not Paris.

quiz.concept: False versus deceptive indications
quiz.q: Shawls arrive at Country B's port bearing a label that is not literally false but is deceptive about where they were made. Looking only at the treaty duties to seize such goods on importation, how does B's position differ if it belongs only to the Paris Convention, compared with belonging to the Madrid Agreement as well?
quiz.ok: Under Paris alone seizure covers only false labels; Madrid adds deceptive ones, so only Madrid reaches them
no: There is no difference, because the Paris seizure rule already reaches any indication that misleads buyers
Madrid would require seizure only if the shawls were wine, as its stronger rules are confined to wine names
Paris requires seizure of deceptive goods too, while Madrid leaves seizure entirely to national courts
quiz.why: Paris Article 10 applies the Article 9 seizure rule only to goods bearing a false indication of source, which the class listed as a limitation. The Madrid Agreement's main improvement was to cover false or deceptive indications, and its Article 1 requires such goods to be seized on importation. A label that is deceptive but not literally false therefore falls outside the Paris seizure rule but inside Madrid's; Madrid's special wine rule concerns genericness, not seizure.

quiz.concept: Madrid: regional wine names never generic
quiz.q: Country B belongs to the Madrid Agreement. Its producers ask B's court to declare two foreign names generic because both are widely used in B: 'Valmonte', a regional name for wine, and 'Korvia', a name for cheese. What may the court do under Madrid?
quiz.ok: It may decide that 'Korvia' has become generic, but it may never treat 'Valmonte' as generic
no: It may declare both generic, since Madrid leaves the question of genericness wholly to national courts
It may declare neither generic, since Madrid bars any finding that a foreign name has become generic
It may declare 'Valmonte' generic but not 'Korvia', since food names get the stronger protection
quiz.why: Madrid Article 4 lets national courts decide which names have become generic, but makes an exception for regional names of wine products, which can never be treated as generic. So B's court may find the cheese name generic on the evidence, but not the wine name. The option barring any genericness finding describes the Lisbon rule for registered appellations, not Madrid, and the 'both' option ignores the wine exception.

quiz.concept: Lisbon: genericness and home protection
quiz.q: 'Brenna blue', a cheese appellation of Country A, is registered at WIPO under the Lisbon Agreement. Cheesemakers in Country B, also a Lisbon member, have used 'Brenna' on their own blue cheese for years and ask B's court to declare it generic. Which change in the facts would allow the court to treat the name as generic?
quiz.ok: Country A's own law stops protecting the appellation at home
no: B's shoppers now use 'Brenna' for any blue cheese, wherever made
Country A's producers stop exporting the cheese to Country B
The name was never entered on Country B's own national register
quiz.why: Under the Lisbon Agreement an appellation must first be recognised and protected at home, is then registered at WIPO's International Bureau so that other members must protect it, and under Article 6 cannot be treated as generic in any member country as long as it stays protected in its home country. Widespread use in B, a halt in exports or the lack of any national entry in B therefore change nothing. Only the loss of protection in Country A lifts the bar on treating the name as generic.

quiz.concept: Extra protection for wine and spirit GIs
quiz.q: 'Castelmora' is a wine GI protected in its home country, E. A winery in Country F, which like E is a WTO member, launched a label last year reading 'Castelmora-style red, produced in F', and its survey shows that no buyer thinks the wine comes from E. Under the protection TRIPS requires for wines and spirits, can Castelmora's producers stop the use in F?
quiz.ok: Yes; the name may not go on wine from elsewhere even with the true origin and 'style' added
no: No; the true origin and the survey show that buyers are not misled, so there is nothing to stop
Yes, but only if they can show that at least some buyers were actually confused about the origin
No; the stronger protection covers spirits only, so a wine name gets only the basic protection
quiz.why: TRIPS Article 23 gives wines and spirits extra protection: their GIs cannot be used for products not from the place even if the true origin is shown, the name is translated, or words like 'kind', 'type', 'style' or 'imitation' are added, and nobody needs to prove that buyers were misled. So F's winery can be stopped despite its accurate label and survey. The 'not misled' option applies the basic Article 22 test, which governs other goods, not wine.

quiz.concept: Literally true but misleading names
quiz.q: 'Neelkot tea' is a registered Indian GI. Country G has a small town that also happens to be called Neelkot, and its tea growers sell 'Neelkot tea' in Country H, a WTO member, in packaging that leads buyers there to think it is the Indian tea. When the Indian producers object in H, the growers argue that the name is literally true about their own town. Under TRIPS, how does that argument fare?
quiz.ok: It fails, because protection reaches a name that is true of the place but falsely suggests another origin
no: It succeeds, because a geographical name that is true of the producers' own town can never be stopped
It fails only if the goods are wines or spirits, since other goods get no protection against true names
It succeeds, because two places sharing one name makes it generic for tea from either of those places
quiz.why: TRIPS Article 22.4 extends protection to a GI that is literally true about the place the goods come from but still falsely makes people think they come from somewhere else; it deals with different places that share a name. G's growers use a true name, but their packaging makes buyers in H think of the Indian tea, so the argument fails. Article 22.4 is part of the basic protection for all GIs, so the wine-only option is wrong.

quiz.concept: No rollback of pre-TRIPS protection
quiz.q: Before TRIPS, Country M barred any use of 'Hiramala', a foreign tea GI protected in its home country, on tea grown elsewhere, even with an accurate origin label. After joining the WTO, M plans to cut this back so that only use that misleads the public is stopped, arguing that this is all TRIPS demands for tea. Is the plan consistent with TRIPS, and why?
quiz.ok: No; a member may not reduce the GI protection it gave before TRIPS, even if above the minimum
no: Yes; TRIPS sets only a minimum for non-wine goods, so M may lower its protection to that level
No; TRIPS requires every member to give all GIs the stronger protection given to wines and spirits
Yes; only wine and spirit GIs keep their pre-TRIPS protection, so tea GIs can be cut back
quiz.why: TRIPS Article 24.3 says a member must not reduce the GI protection it already gave before TRIPS. M is right that the basic level for tea only requires stopping misleading use and unfair competition, but the standstill rule stops it lowering the higher protection it already gave. The option claiming that all GIs get wine-level protection reaches the right answer for the wrong reason: extending that protection to all products is still unresolved at the WTO.

quiz.concept: Prior use exception: either route suffices
quiz.q: Since 1990 a distillery in Country N has used, continuously and in good faith, a spirit GI belonging to Country P; both countries are WTO members. Country P demands that N stop the use. A student says N must comply because the use had not lasted 10 years before 15 April 1994. Is the student right, and why?
quiz.ok: No; good faith use before that date is enough on its own, so N need not stop it
no: Yes; the exception requires both ten years of use and good faith before that date
No; any use begun before TRIPS applied is protected, whether in good faith or not
Yes; the exception for continued use covers wine names only, never spirit names
quiz.why: TRIPS Article 24.4 lets a member allow its people to continue using another member's wine or spirit GI if they used it continuously either for at least 10 years before 15 April 1994, or in good faith before that date; either route is enough. N's distillery began in good faith in 1990, so it qualifies through the second route even though it falls short of 10 years. The notes flag the 'both conditions' reading as an error in the class notes, and use for under 10 years without good faith would not qualify.

quiz.concept: Good faith trade marks are grandfathered
quiz.q: Rosa Foods registered 'Ambavali' as a trade mark for pickles in Country S, a WTO member, in good faith and years before Ambavali pickles were protected as a GI in India. Rosa's pickles are made elsewhere, and buyers in S take them for Ambavali pickles. The Ambavali producers try to cancel the mark in S, relying on TRIPS, and fail. Which change in the facts would have changed that result?
quiz.ok: Rosa had picked the name knowing of the Ambavali pickles' fame, in order to trade on it
no: Rosa had only applied for, and not yet registered, the mark before the GI was protected
Country S had begun applying TRIPS only after Rosa had registered its mark
The Ambavali pickles had since become far better known in S than Rosa's own brand
quiz.why: TRIPS Article 24.5 protects trade marks applied for, registered or used in good faith before TRIPS applied, or before the GI was protected in its home country. Rosa's mark contains the GI and misleads buyers in S, which would otherwise require cancellation under Article 22.3, but it was registered in good faith before India protected the GI, so it survives. Had Rosa chosen the name to trade on the pickles' fame, the good faith shield would be gone and Article 22.3 would apply; a good faith application alone, or registration before TRIPS applied in S, would still have protected the mark, and later fame changes nothing.

quiz.concept: The two-level problem
quiz.q: An Indian exporter finds that a firm in Country Z, a WTO member, sells 'Basmati-style rice, grown in Z', with its true origin clearly shown. The exporter's manager says Z must ban the label outright under TRIPS, just as it would have to ban 'Champagne-style wine, made in Z'. What is the best assessment?
quiz.ok: He is wrong: rice gets only basic protection, so misleading use or unfair competition must be shown
no: He is right: TRIPS gives every GI the same absolute protection, whatever the product happens to be
He is wrong: Basmati is not a place name, so it cannot be protected as a GI abroad at all
He is right: a clear origin label can never protect a firm that uses another country's GI
quiz.why: TRIPS has two levels: wines and spirits get Article 23 protection, which bans use even with the true origin or words like 'style', while other products get only the Article 22 level, where the owner must show that the use misleads the public or is unfair competition. Basmati is rice (and a registered GI, though not a place name), so the comparison with Champagne fails and a clear origin label may defeat the claim. This gap is why India has long sought to extend Article 23 protection to all products, an issue still unresolved at the WTO.

quiz.concept: Who grandfathering protects
quiz.q: A US distiller is launching a new whisky brand this year. Relying on a class note, 'Uncle Sam + Scotch Whiskey = Allowed', and on the 2006 EU and US agreement on semi-generic names, it plans to label the whisky 'Uncle Sam Scotch Whiskey'. What is the best assessment?
quiz.ok: It fails: only existing users within an exception may carry on, and the 2006 deal covers only wine
no: It succeeds: putting a prefix such as 'Uncle Sam' before the GI makes it a new, lawful trade mark
It succeeds: the 2006 agreement lets US labels keep European names as long as the true origin is shown
It fails: whisky names can never be used outside Scotland, whatever exception the user claims
quiz.why: A grandfather clause lets an existing user carry on while new users are banned; in GI law it appears in TRIPS Article 24.4 (long prior use of wine and spirit names), Article 24.5 (prior good faith trade marks) and the 2006 EU and US wine agreement. A brand launched this year has no prior use or prior mark, the 2006 agreement covers wine names only, and US rules recognise Scotch whisky as a distinctive product of Scotland. The prefix option repeats the class memory aid, which is wrong as law because Article 23.1 bans a spirit GI on other spirits even with extra words added.

quiz.concept: What follows from semi-generic status
quiz.q: In 2004 Arjun, advising a Californian winery, says that 'Chablis' in the US is a generic word just like 'French fries', so the winery may print 'Chablis' on its own on any white wine. Which statement of the position is most accurate?
quiz.ok: It was semi-generic: usable on other wine only with the true origin beside it and the type standard met
no: It was fully generic, so the winery could print 'Chablis' on its own, provided the wine was white
It was a protected GI, so wine from outside Chablis could never carry the name anywhere in the US
It was semi-generic, so other wine could use it freely, provided no buyer was actually misled by it
quiz.why: A semi-generic name still has geographic meaning but is also used in the US as the name of a class or type of wine; Chablis is one of the 16 names on the slides. Even before the 2006 agreement, US law allowed such a name on wine from elsewhere only if the true place of origin appeared right next to it, as in 'California Champagne', and the wine met the standard for that type. Arjun treats Chablis like 'French fries', a name with no geographic meaning left, and misses that its use was regulated.

quiz.concept: The 2006 grandfather cut-off
quiz.q: Two Californian wineries label sparkling wine 'California Champagne', with the origin next to the name and the wine meeting the type standard. Redwood Cellars' label, under its brand 'Redwood', was approved in 2003; Bluebird Wines first sought approval for its 'Bluebird' label in 2009. Under the rule the 2006 agreement set, which winery may use 'Champagne', and on what basis?
quiz.ok: Redwood alone, since only labels approved before the agreement may continue, under the same brand
no: Both, because each states its true origin right next to the name, as US law had always required
Neither, because the agreement reserved Champagne for French wine with no exceptions at all
Redwood alone, since a winery already using the name may carry on with it under any brand
quiz.why: The 2006 agreement committed the US to change its law so that these semi-generic names may be used only on wine from the relevant EU country, with a grandfather exception for labels approved by a COLA before 10 March 2006, and then only under the same brand name. Redwood's 2003 approval brings it within the exception, but Bluebird's label came too late, so stating the origin next to the name no longer helps it. The 'both' option applies the pre-agreement US rule, and the 'any brand' option picks the right winery for the wrong reason: the right is tied to the brand on the approved label, not to the winery.

quiz.concept: The right follows the brand
quiz.q: Harbour Vineyards holds a pre-agreement label approval for 'Seagull Serenade California Cream Sherry'. It sells the Seagull brand to Tern Wines and starts selling its own wine under a new brand, 'Albatross'. Who may now use 'Sherry' under the grandfather exception?
quiz.ok: Tern, on Seagull labels within the same limits, but not Harbour on its Albatross wine
no: Harbour on its Albatross wine, since the right belongs to whoever obtained the approval
Neither, since selling the brand ends the grandfather right for any later owner of it
Both, since Harbour keeps its own right and Tern gains a fresh one on Seagull labels
quiz.why: The grandfather right follows the label, meaning the brand name, not the company: when a brand is sold, the buyer and any later owner get the same rights and restrictions, as with Company B in the Smith example. A new brand is a new label, so Harbour's Albatross wine cannot use 'Sherry'. The tempting idea that the right stays with the company that obtained the COLA is exactly what the exam tip rejects: change the brand and the right is lost.

quiz.concept: What the grandfather right freezes
quiz.q: Oakleaf Wines holds a pre-agreement label approval for 'Oakleaf Velvet California Ruby Port': Oakleaf is the brand, Velvet the fanciful name, Port the class and type, and California the stated origin. Which planned change would cost Oakleaf the right to keep using 'Port' on this wine?
quiz.ok: Renaming the Velvet line 'Midnight' but keeping the Oakleaf brand
no: Changing the stated origin from California to Sonoma County
Dropping the word 'Ruby' from the label but changing nothing else
Redesigning the label's artwork while keeping every name on it
quiz.why: Under the 2006 grandfather exception an old label may keep the semi-generic name only if it carries the same brand name, or the same brand name and fanciful name, shown on the pre-agreement COLA. Only those names are frozen, so changing Velvet to Midnight loses the right, just as Elegance becoming Robust did in the Smith example. Updating the stated origin, as with California becoming Napa Valley, is allowed because the origin is not frozen, and dropping a word like 'Cream' or 'Ruby' leaves the frozen names intact.

quiz.concept: Applicant represents producers, need not produce
quiz.q: A state leather development corporation, set up under a state law, applies for a GI for Mohangarh chappals on behalf of the region's cobblers. An objector argues that the corporation has never made a single chappal and so cannot be the applicant. Is the objection sound?
quiz.ok: No, because the test is whether the applicant represents the producers' interest, not whether it makes the goods itself.
no: Yes, because an applicant must itself make the goods, and a body that makes none cannot speak for those who do.
No, because any body set up under a law may apply, whether or not it represents the producers of the goods.
Yes, because a statutory corporation can be entered only as an authorised user in Part B, never as proprietor in Part A.
quiz.why: Under section 11(1) the question is whether the applicant represents the interest of the producers, not whether it produces anything itself, which is why statutory bodies such as the Tea Board, APEDA, LIDCOM and LIDKAR hold GIs as proprietors. The Toda Embroidery decision makes the same point, so the objection fails if the corporation genuinely represents the cobblers. The 'any body set up under a law' option reaches the right result for the wrong reason, because being created by statute is not enough without representing the producers.

quiz.concept: Who counts as a producer
quiz.q: Dhanpur district is known for its rice and for wild honey from the Bansvan forest. Arun only processes and packs rice grown by his neighbours, and Bela only collects honey from the forest. Each product's GI applicant must represent the interest of its producers. Which of the two counts as a producer?
quiz.ok: Both: processing and packing count for agricultural goods, and collecting counts as exploiting natural goods.
no: Neither: only those who grow a crop or make an article are producers, not those who merely pack or collect.
Only Bela: processing and packing are trading steps, which the Act keeps separate from producing the goods.
Only Arun: natural goods are gathered rather than produced, so wild honey has no producers to represent.
quiz.why: Section 2(1)(k) defines a producer by the type of goods: for agricultural goods it includes one who processes or packages them, for natural goods one who exploits them, for example by extracting or collecting, and for handicraft or industrial goods one who makes them. Arun is therefore a producer of rice and Bela of honey. The 'only Bela' option fails twice over, because the definition expressly covers processing and packaging, and it also includes anyone who trades or deals in the production.

quiz.concept: Unregistered producer must join Part B
quiz.q: Lata weaves Tamrapur sarees inside the GI area but has never applied to be entered in Part B of the register. She finds a Delhi shop selling machine-made fakes as 'Tamrapur sarees' and wants to sue for infringement. What is the best advice?
quiz.ok: She cannot sue unless she registers in Part B as an authorised user, though the registered proprietor could sue now.
no: She can sue, provided she proves that she is a genuine producer who weaves the sarees inside the GI area.
She cannot sue, because only the proprietor in Part A, never an individual producer, can bring an infringement suit.
She can sue, because the registration certificate is prima facie evidence of validity that any producer may rely on.
quiz.why: Part A records the GI and its proprietor, while Part B records the individual producers who apply under section 17 and are registered as authorised users; only the registered proprietor and the authorised users can sue for infringement (section 21(1)(a)). Lata is a genuine producer but is not registered, so she must join Part B or leave the suit to the proprietor. The Part A-only option is wrong because authorised users can sue in their own right, and being a genuine producer is not enough without registration.

quiz.concept: Standards must show place-linked quality
quiz.q: An association of cement makers in one district applies for a GI. As its standards benchmark it relies only on the fact that every member's cement meets a well-known international ISO quality standard. How should the Registry view this benchmark?
quiz.ok: As inadequate, because an ISO standard shows uniform industrial quality, not quality due to the place.
no: As beside the point, because industrial goods such as cement can never be registered as GIs in India.
As sufficient, because India checks goods only against whatever standards the applicant chooses to set.
As irrelevant, because only a statutory authority, not a private association, may apply for industrial goods.
quiz.why: The application must explain how the goods' quality, reputation or other characteristic is due exclusively or essentially to the area's natural and human factors, and Rule 32(6)(b) asks for standards that show this place-linked quality. A general ISO standard measures uniform quality that could be achieved anywhere, so on its own it cannot prove the link a GI needs. The 'sufficient' option misreads the point that India examines goods only against the application's specifications: those standards must themselves show the place link. Industrial goods can be GIs, since the definition of producer expressly covers them, and associations of producers may apply.

quiz.concept: Genericness judged at origin and market
quiz.q: Objectors to a GI for Ambapur pickle survey buyers in the big cities where most of it is sold, and show that 'Ambapur' is now used there for any spicy mango pickle. The Registry looks no further and refuses the application on the ground that the name is generic. What is the strongest criticism of the refusal?
quiz.ok: It ignored how the name is understood in Ambapur, which must be weighed along with the markets.
no: It looked at the wrong place, since only the meaning in Ambapur, where the name originated, can count.
It treated the name as generic, though a name that once identified a place can never become generic.
It applied the genericness bar, which is meant only for foreign names that are no longer used at home.
quiz.why: Section 9 bars generic names, and its Explanation tells the Registry to consider the situation both in the place where the name originated and in the area where the goods are consumed. By relying only on city usage, the Registry left out half of that test, since Ambapur's own understanding of the name had to be weighed too. The 'only Ambapur counts' option overcorrects, because the markets where the pickle is consumed are equally part of the test; and genericness is a separate limb from the bar on foreign GIs that are dead at home, as 'French fries' type names show.

quiz.concept: Foreign GI unprotected at home
quiz.q: Two foreign producers' associations apply in India, and each name otherwise meets the Act's requirements. 'Valmora' cheese is still protected at home but little known in India. 'Tolvanna' cheese is famous among Indian buyers, but its home country stopped protecting the name years ago and producers there no longer use it. Which can be registered?
quiz.ok: Only Valmora, since a name unprotected or out of use at home is barred, however famous it is in India.
no: Only Tolvanna, since registration in India turns on how well Indian buyers know a name, not on home law.
Both, since Indian registration depends only on Indian law, so the home country's position is irrelevant.
Neither, since foreign names cannot be GIs in India and can be protected here only through passing off.
quiz.why: Section 9 bars a GI that is not protected, has stopped being protected, or has fallen into disuse in its home country; the notes call these foreign GIs that are dead at home. Tolvanna is dead at home, so its fame in India cannot save it, while Valmora is still protected at home and meets the other requirements. The 'both' option forgets that the home-country bar is itself part of Indian law, and 'neither' is wrong because foreign GIs can be registered in India, as CIVC's Indian registration of Champagne shows.

quiz.concept: Use contrary to law bars registration
quiz.q: A hill community applies for a GI for its ceremonial caps, which are made from the feathers of a bird protected under wildlife law. The caps are famous, made with special local skill and clearly linked to the region. What is the strongest ground for refusing registration?
quiz.ok: Using the indication on such caps would be contrary to a law in force, and reputation cannot cure that.
no: The name is likely to deceive buyers, since they may not realise that protected birds' feathers are used.
The caps contain matter likely to hurt religious feelings, because they are worn at religious ceremonies.
There is none, since the bars concern only the words of the indication, and this name is lawful in itself.
quiz.why: Section 9 bars an indication whose use would be contrary to any law in force; the notes give caps made from the feathers of protected birds as an illustration, because they may clash with the Wild Life (Protection) Act, 1972. A strong reputation and local link cannot cure that illegality. The option saying the bars concern only the words is the tempting error: the bar asks whether use of the indication would break the law, which turns on the goods it is used for, not just the words.

quiz.concept: Conditions for homonymous GIs
quiz.q: Neelgaon shawls from a northern district are a registered GI. Weavers in a southern district of another state, also called Neelgaon, apply for their own Neelgaon GI for a different kind of shawl, proposing labels that name their state. The northern proprietor objects. Which objection, if proved, gives the strongest ground for refusal?
quiz.ok: Even with the state named on the labels, buyers would still take the southern shawls for northern ones.
no: The northern GI was registered first, and the first GI for a name keeps it for that place alone.
The northern proprietor has not agreed, and a second GI for the same name needs the first one's licence.
Whatever the state labels say, a literally true name that sounds like another GI is always barred.
quiz.why: Section 10 allows a homonymous GI to be registered if the Registrar is satisfied that practical conditions, such as clear labels, will keep the two apart, that the producers of both places are treated equitably, and that consumers will not be confused or misled; Rule 32(6)(h) makes the applicant explain these differences and protective measures. Proof that buyers would still be misled despite the state labels defeats the third condition, so it is the strongest objection. Being registered first gives no veto, because the Act expressly allows a second GI with the same name, and consent cannot be required when a GI cannot be licensed at all.

quiz.concept: Opposition standing versus rectification standing
quiz.q: Farah, a consumer activist with no business interest in tea, believes a newly advertised GI application for Girikund tea draws the area's boundary dishonestly. She may also want to attack the registration later if it goes through. Which advice on her standing is correct?
quiz.ok: She may oppose now, as any person can, but to seek rectification after registration she must show she is a person aggrieved.
no: She may oppose now and seek rectification later, because both routes are open to any person, whatever their interest.
She can do neither, because only producers of the area or their bodies may object to a GI at any stage.
She must show she is a person aggrieved to oppose now, but any person may seek rectification once it is registered.
quiz.why: After advertisement in the GI Journal any person may oppose within 3 months, extendable by 1 month, but after registration only a person aggrieved can apply under section 27 to cancel or correct the entry. So Farah's lack of a business interest does not stop an opposition, though it may defeat a later rectification, which is exactly where the Tirupati Laddu challenge failed. The 'both routes open to anyone' option ignores this difference in standing between the two stages.

quiz.concept: Lapse, late renewal and authorised users
quiz.q: The Mirapur chilli GI reached the end of its ten-year term last month and the proprietor forgot to renew it. Nisha, registered as an authorised user only three years ago, says her own registration still has seven years to run, so the lapse does not affect her. Which statement is correct?
quiz.ok: Her registration cannot outlast the GI's, but the proprietor can still renew late within six months by paying an extra fee.
no: Her registration runs its full ten years, since an authorised user's term is independent of the GI's own term.
Her registration ends with the GI's, and the GI is lost for good, since a lapsed GI can never be renewed or restored.
She can keep the GI alive herself by taking an assignment of it from the proprietor who failed to renew it.
quiz.why: An authorised user's registration lasts 10 years or until the GI registration ends, whichever is earlier, so Nisha cannot rely on her own seven years. The GI is renewable for 10 years at a time (section 18), a late renewal is still possible within six months of expiry on paying an extra fee, and even a GI removed for non-renewal can be restored on application.
