The option saying the GI is lost for good gets the first half right but ignores late renewal and restoration, and assignment is impossible because section 24 bars any assignment of a GI.

quiz.concept: Farming method and the Indian specification
quiz.q: The registered specification for Dhanpur rice describes the variety, the area and the grain's qualities, but says nothing about farming methods. One authorised user argues that another, who grows the rice with chemical fertilisers, cannot lawfully sell it as Dhanpur rice. Is the argument sound?
quiz.ok: No, because the goods are judged only against the registered specification, not an assumed farming method.
no: Yes, because a GI implies traditional organic farming, as the EU's concern with production inputs shows.
Yes, because Indian law examines the whole production process from scratch against a detailed specification.
No, because Indian law does not allow a specification to say anything about how the goods are produced.
quiz.why: In India the Registry examines the goods only against the specifications in the application, and the method of cultivation usually does not matter, for example organic or chemical farming of Basmati; in the EU, inputs such as milk quality and fodder do matter. Dhanpur's specification sets no farming method, so rice grown with chemical fertilisers still meets it. The organic-farming option imports the EU approach, and the option saying a specification cannot address production is wrong because an Indian application must set out a standards benchmark: the standards for producing or making the goods.

quiz.concept: Control body: EU condition, Indian option
quiz.q: Two producer groups, one in India and one in an EU member state, each apply at home to register a cheese GI. Each application sets out detailed production standards and how members will keep quality consistent, but neither names any body that will inspect compliance. How does that gap affect each application?
quiz.ok: Only the EU application fails a condition of registration; India asks for an inspection structure only if one exists.
no: Both applications fail a condition of registration, since every GI system requires a named body to check compliance.
Neither application fails any condition, since quality checking is left everywhere to the period after registration.
Only the Indian application fails a condition, since India, unlike the EU, examines the whole process from scratch.
quiz.why: In the EU a named control body must check compliance and controls are a condition of registration, whereas an Indian application only has to describe the inspection structure 'if any' (section 11(2) and Rule 32(6)), alongside its mechanism for maintaining quality. So the Indian group can proceed without an inspection body, which is why weak checking after registration is one of the main criticisms of the Indian system. The inverted option wrongly gives India the EU's practice of examining the whole process from scratch against a detailed product specification.

quiz.concept: Authorised users cannot exclude each other
quiz.q: Anand Farms and Bimal Farms are both registered authorised users of the Kesarpur saffron GI. Anand, registered five years before Bimal, sues Bimal for infringement, claiming that its exclusive right to use the GI on saffron is being invaded. Will the suit succeed?
quiz.ok: No: no authorised user can stop another merely because of registration, though each can act against outsiders.
no: Yes: the earlier authorised user gains priority, so a later user's use invades the earlier user's exclusive right.
Yes: each authorised user's exclusive right to use the GI binds everyone, including the other authorised users.
No: only the registered proprietor, not an authorised user, can bring a suit for infringement against anyone.
quiz.why: Section 21(1)(b) gives authorised users the exclusive right to use the GI on the registered goods, but section 21(3) says that where there are several authorised users none can stop the others merely because of registration; each has the same rights against outsiders. So Anand's suit fails, and its earlier registration gives it no priority. The option saying only the proprietor can sue reaches the right result for a wrong reason, because section 21(1)(a) lets authorised users as well as the proprietor sue for infringement.

quiz.concept: Unregistered GI: passing off only
quiz.q: Corvane is a wine region abroad whose name is protected as a GI at home but has never been registered in India. An Indian winery starts selling 'Corvane Valley' wine, and the Corvane producers' association wants to stop it in an Indian court. Which route is open to it?
quiz.ok: A passing off action, since an unregistered GI cannot found an infringement suit but passing off is preserved.
no: An infringement suit, since wines are notified goods and so receive the extra protection even if unregistered.
No civil route, since the Act protects only registered GIs and expressly shuts out every other kind of claim.
An infringement suit, since registration is only prima facie evidence and proof of reputation can replace it.
quiz.why: Section 20(1) bars an infringement suit based on an unregistered GI, while section 20(2) keeps the passing off action open; the Scotch Whisky case used this route. The extra protection for notified goods is a form of infringement of a registered GI, so the fact that wines are notified does not help a name that is not registered in India. The prima facie evidence option confuses the evidential effect of a registration certificate with the need to be registered at all.

quiz.concept: Why a GI cannot be licensed
quiz.q: A multinational offers the proprietor of the Pashmigarh shawl GI a large royalty for a licence to use the GI on shawls it will weave inside the GI area to the registered standards. A trade mark owner could sign such a deal. What best explains why the GI proprietor cannot?
quiz.ok: A GI belongs to the place and its producer community, so it is not an asset the proprietor can deal in.
no: The proprietor alone answers for the goods' quality, and a licence would put quality outside its control.
A licence must first be approved by the Registrar and entered on the register, and none has been sought.
Only registered authorised users may take a licence of a GI, and the multinational has not been registered.
quiz.why: Section 24 bars assignment, transmission, licensing, pledge, mortgage or any similar agreement over a GI, because a GI belongs to a place and its community rather than to a company; the proprietor is only the channel through which the benefit reaches the community. This is why the argument in Tea Board v ITC that ITC should have taken a licence failed. The quality option is wrong because the notes stress that the proprietor by itself is not responsible for maintaining quality, and no approval or registration can make a GI licence valid, whoever the licensee is.

quiz.concept: Succession on death versus sale
quiz.q: Gopal and Hari are authorised users of the Tamrapur saree GI. Gopal dies, and his daughter Meena inherits and carries on his loom business. Hari sells his workshop to a Mumbai company, and the sale deed says that 'Hari's GI right' passes to the buyer. Which is correct?
quiz.ok: Meena succeeds to Gopal's right on his death, but the sale deed cannot pass Hari's right to the company.
no: Both transfers are effective, since an authorised user's right passes with the business, like goodwill.
Neither is effective, since a GI right ends with the authorised user and cannot pass to anyone, even on death.
The sale is effective, but Meena must apply afresh, since rights pass by agreement and not on death.
quiz.why: Section 24 bars assignment, transmission, licensing and similar agreements over a GI, with one exception: when an authorised user dies, the right passes to the successor in title. Meena takes Gopal's right as his successor, but Hari's sale deed is an assignment and cannot carry the GI right to the company. The goodwill option treats a GI like a trade mark, which is exactly the difference the notes stress.

quiz.concept: Suggestive signs misleading about origin
quiz.q: A Delhi trader packs saffron grown outside Kesarpur in boxes that never use the word 'Kesarpur'. Instead they show Kesarpur's famous hilltop fort and the words 'from the valley of the fort', and buyers take the saffron to be Kesarpur saffron. Does this infringe the registered GI?
quiz.ok: Yes, because using anything that suggests the GI so as to mislead buyers about origin is enough.
no: No, because infringement needs use of the registered word itself, and the trader never used it.
Yes, but only if saffron is a notified good, since mere suggestion is caught only by the extra protection.
No, because pictures of a real place are free for anyone to use, whatever goods they are printed on.
quiz.why: Section 22(1)(a) is infringed by a person who is not an authorised user and who uses the GI, or anything that suggests it, so that buyers are misled about where the goods come from. The fort picture and slogan suggest Kesarpur and do mislead buyers, so the trader infringes even though the word itself is absent. The 'notified goods' option is wrong because the general rule already covers suggestion that misleads, and saffron has not been notified anyway.

quiz.concept: True origin, misleading manufacturing process
quiz.q: The Tamrapur saree GI is registered for hand-woven sarees, and its specification requires weaving by hand. Ravi, who runs a power-loom unit inside Tamrapur and is not an authorised user, sells his machine-made sarees as 'Tamrapur sarees', and buyers assume they are hand-woven. What is the proprietor's best line of attack?
quiz.ok: Unfair competition, as the use misleads buyers about the manufacturing process though the origin is true.
no: None, since goods really made inside the GI area may carry the area's name whatever their method of making.
Misleading use about origin, since only goods made by authorised users count as coming from the GI area.
The extra protection for notified goods, since true origin defeats every other kind of infringement claim.
quiz.why: Section 22(1)(b) treats unfair competition as infringement, and one listed type is use that misleads about the nature, manufacturing process or characteristics of the goods. Ravi's sarees truly come from Tamrapur, so misleading use about origin under section 22(1)(a) fits poorly, but selling power-loom sarees under a GI whose specification requires hand weaving misleads buyers about the process. The 'none' option borrows the point that the method of making usually does not matter in India, but goods are measured against the specification, and this one requires hand weaving. The 'origin' option stretches origin to mean authorised production, and the notified-goods route is closed because sarees are not notified.

quiz.concept: Literally true name that misleads
quiz.q: Suryagarh brass lamps are a registered GI for a district in Odisha. A maker in a Rajasthan town that is also called Suryagarh labels its brass lamps 'Genuine Suryagarh Brass', which is true of its own town, and buyers take them to be the Odisha lamps. Is this infringement?
quiz.ok: Yes: a name true of the seller's own town infringes if it makes buyers think the goods come from the GI area.
no: No: a place name that is literally true of where the goods are actually made can never be misleading in law.
No: the Odisha proprietor's only remedy is to oppose any GI application that the Rajasthan makers may later file.
Yes, but only if the Rajasthan maker also copies the shape and design of the Odisha lamps.
quiz.why: Section 22(1)(c) treats as infringement the use of another GI that is literally true about its own place but makes buyers think the goods come from the area of the registered GI. 'Genuine Suryagarh Brass' is true of the Rajasthan town but leads buyers to believe the lamps are from Odisha, so it infringes. The 'literally true' option is the very argument this rule closes, and copying the design is not needed because a GI protects the name used on goods.

quiz.concept: Notified goods: no proof of misleading
quiz.q: Suppose Montaval is a registered GI for wine and Pashmigarh a registered GI for shawls. A Nashik winery sells 'Montaval-style wine, made in Nashik', and a Ludhiana mill sells 'Pashmigarh-type shawl, made in Ludhiana'. How do the two labels fare?
quiz.ok: The winery infringes despite stating the true origin; the mill only if misleading use or unfair competition is proved.
no: Both infringe outright, since adding 'style' or 'type' to any registered GI is barred whatever the kind of goods.
Neither infringes, since each label states the true origin, so no buyer can be misled about where the goods were really made.
The mill infringes outright and the winery only on proof, since shawls are notified goods and wines are not.
quiz.why: Sections 22(2) and 22(3) give notified goods extra protection: using another GI on goods not from that place infringes even if the true origin is shown or words like 'style' or 'type' are added, and the only notification covers wines and spirits. So the winery infringes without proof that anyone was misled, while the shawl label must be attacked under section 22(1), where stating the true origin makes misleading use harder to prove. The inverted option swaps the goods that have actually been notified.

quiz.concept: Extra protection needs a notification
quiz.q: A student writes: "India goes further than TRIPS by giving the extra protection to all goods, not just wines and spirits, so a seller of 'Kolhapuri style' chappals automatically infringes the Kolhapuri Chappal GI." What is the main flaw in this reasoning?
quiz.ok: India can extend it to any goods, but only by Central Government notification, and only wines and spirits are notified.
no: India's Act confines the extra protection to wines and spirits, exactly as TRIPS does, so it has no power to go further.
The extra protection catches words such as 'kind' or 'imitation' but does not reach the word 'style' at all.
Kolhapuri Chappal has never been registered as a GI, so no protection of any kind is available to its makers.
quiz.why: Section 22(2) lets the Central Government extend the extra protection to any goods, but only by notification, and the only notification found (1 October 2010) covers wines and spirits; this is one of the listed common mistakes. So 'Kolhapuri style' chappals do not automatically infringe, though the proprietor can still sue under section 22(1) if it proves misleading use or unfair competition. The option confining India's power to wines and spirits is wrong because India's power covers any goods; what is limited is its use of that power.

quiz.concept: Resale of genuine goods and impairment
quiz.q: Two Mumbai traders buy genuine Kesarpur saffron from authorised users. Trader A repacks it into small tins labelled 'Kesarpur saffron'. Trader B keeps his stock in a damp godown until it loses colour and aroma, then sells it under the same name. Which trader can rely on the freedom to resell genuine goods?
quiz.ok: Only A, because the freedom does not cover goods whose condition was impaired after they were put on the market.
no: Both, because the saffron in each case is genuine and truly comes from Kesarpur, which is all that matters.
Neither, because repacking or reselling GI goods under the GI name is a right reserved to authorised users.
Only B, because B sold the saffron in its original form, while A altered its packaging and presentation.
quiz.why: Under section 22(4) a person who lawfully buys genuine GI goods may resell, process or repack them without infringing, unless their condition is impaired after they were put on the market. A's repacking is like repacking genuine Darjeeling tea into smaller packets, which is allowed, but B's damp storage impaired the saffron's condition, so B loses the protection. The 'both' option ignores this exception, which is the whole limit on the resale freedom.

quiz.concept: Bad faith and the five-year limit
quiz.q: Hilltop Foods, whose founder grew up in Kesarpur, had its trade mark 'Kesarpur Kitchen' for packaged sweets published and then registered in 2016. The Kesarpur saffron GI's proprietor learnt of it in 2019 and sued in 2023, and the suit is met with the five-year limit. Which one change in the facts would most help the proprietor?
quiz.ok: Evidence that Hilltop chose the mark in bad faith, to trade on the reputation of the saffron GI.
no: Evidence that the proprietor actually learnt of the mark only in 2020, a year later than it first claimed.
Evidence that Hilltop is still using the mark every day, right up to the date the suit was filed.
Evidence that the proprietor sent Hilltop a warning letter every year from 2019 onwards.
quiz.why: Section 26(4) bars action against the use or registration of a trade mark five years after the earlier of two dates, the date the GI proprietor or user learnt of it and the date of registration if the mark had been published by then, but the protection is lost if the mark was used or registered in bad faith. Registration and publication in 2016 came first, so time ran out in 2021 whether knowledge came in 2019 or 2020, and only bad faith would reopen the claim. Continuing use does not restart the clock, as Tea Board v ITC held, and warning letters do not move the dates from which time runs: the Tea Board wrote to ITC in 2005, 2006 and 2008, and its 2010 suit was still barred.

quiz.concept: Trade mark refusal for misleading GI
quiz.q: A company applies to register the trade mark 'Kesarpur Gold' for saffron grown far from Kesarpur, and its use would mislead buyers about origin. The proprietor of the Kesarpur saffron GI has not objected and may never hear of the application. Can the Registrar of Trade Marks refuse it?
quiz.ok: Yes: the Registrar must refuse such a mark on his own, without waiting for any interested party to object.
no: No: only the GI proprietor can block the mark, and it must do so by filing an opposition in time.
No: only the GI Registry may act to protect a registered GI, so the Trade Marks Registrar has no role.
Yes, but only if saffron is a notified good, since marks containing a GI are barred only for notified goods.
quiz.why: Section 25 requires the Registrar of Trade Marks, on his own or at the request of an interested party, to refuse or cancel a trade mark that contains a GI for goods not from that place where the use would mislead, or that contains a GI for notified goods. Here the use would mislead, so the mark must be refused even though no one has objected and saffron is not notified. The 'notified goods only' option forgets the first limb of the rule, which covers any goods where the use misleads.

quiz.concept: Good-faith prior marks: GI filing cut-off
quiz.q: The producers' body applied for the Dhanpur rice GI in March 2020, and it was registered in 2022. In June 2021 a miller, who had never used the name before and did not know of the GI application, applied in good faith to register 'Dhanpur Grain' as a trade mark for rice. Can the miller rely on the protection for prior good-faith trade marks?
quiz.ok: No: it covers only marks adopted before the GI application was filed, and the GI dates from March 2020.
no: Yes: the miller applied in June 2021, which was still before the GI was actually entered on the register.
Yes: a trade mark adopted in good faith stays valid whenever it was applied for, used or registered.
No: any trade mark containing a GI is invalid in every case, whatever its date and whatever the good faith.
quiz.why: Section 26(1) saves a trade mark containing a GI that was applied for, registered or used in good faith before the Act came into force or before the GI application was filed, and a registered GI counts as registered from its application date. The miller applied in June 2021, after the March 2020 GI application, so the protection does not apply. The tempting option measures time from actual registration, which is the wrong cut-off, and the option calling every such mark invalid ignores that the protection for prior marks exists at all.

quiz.concept: Own-name use and its limit
quiz.q: Ramesh Kesarpuria runs a spice business founded by his grandfather. He uses 'R. Kesarpuria & Sons, Spice Merchants' on his shop sign, and also sells saffron grown elsewhere in boxes printing 'KESARPURIA' in large letters styled like Kesarpur saffron packs, so that buyers take it for Kesarpur saffron. Which use is protected?
quiz.ok: The shop sign is protected but the boxes are not, because own-name use is lost where it confuses or misleads.
no: Both are protected, because a trader may always use his own family name, whatever impression it creates.
Neither is protected, because a family name containing a GI can never be used for any goods or business.
The boxes are protected but the shop sign is not, because the own-name rule covers goods, not trade names.
quiz.why: Section 26(3) lets a person use their own name, or the name of their predecessor in business, unless the use confuses or misleads. The shop sign is an ordinary use of Ramesh's family name, but the boxes are designed to make buyers think the saffron is Kesarpur saffron, so the defence fails there. The 'always' option ignores the limit built into the rule, and the inverted option has the rule backwards, since it protects a person's own name in business.

quiz.concept: Innocent infringer: nominal damages only
quiz.q: The Pashmigarh shawl proprietor sues two traders who sold fake 'Pashmigarh' shawls. Xavier had no idea the GI was registered and stopped the day he was told; Yusuf knew and carried on for a year. The proprietor claims both damages and an account of profits from each. What money relief can it get?
quiz.ok: Only nominal damages from Xavier; from Yusuf, damages or an account of profits, at the proprietor's choice.
no: Full damages and an account of profits from both, since liability for infringement does not depend on knowledge.
Nothing from Xavier, since innocent use is no infringement; both damages and profits from Yusuf.
Damages or an account of profits from both, at the proprietor's choice, since knowledge affects only costs.
quiz.why: The court can grant an injunction, damages or an account of profits at the plaintiff's choice, and delivery up (section 67); but where the defendant acted innocently and stopped as soon as he knew of the GI, only nominal damages are given. Xavier fits that description, while Yusuf knowingly carried on, so against Yusuf the proprietor must choose between damages and profits. The option giving both remedies against Yusuf ignores that they are alternatives, and the option giving nothing against Xavier wrongly treats innocence as a defence to infringement, when the rule only limits him to nominal damages.

quiz.concept: Seller's defence to false GI offence
quiz.q: Meera's shop sold sarees falsely labelled as Tamrapur sarees. She had bought them from a regular wholesaler on invoices certifying them genuine, checked the labels, had no reason to suspect them, and at once gave the police the wholesaler's details. She is prosecuted for selling goods with a false GI. Is she likely to be convicted?
quiz.ok: No: selling such goods is an offence, but a seller who took care and named her supplier has a defence.
no: Yes: selling goods bearing a false GI is an offence whatever care the seller took before selling them.
No: only a person who falsifies a GI or applies it to goods commits an offence, never a mere seller.
Yes, but since she acted innocently, the court can order her to pay only nominal damages.
quiz.why: Section 40 makes selling, hiring or keeping for sale goods with a false GI an offence carrying the same punishment as falsification, but gives defences where reasonable precautions were taken, the supplier is disclosed, or the accused acted innocently. Meera's checks, her lack of any reason to suspect the goods and her prompt disclosure of the wholesaler meet these defences, so she should be acquitted. The 'mere seller' option reaches the right result for the wrong reason, since selling is itself an offence, and nominal damages belong to civil remedies, not criminal liability.

quiz.concept: Rectification route after the IPAB
quiz.q: The Bansvan honey GI was registered in 2019. In 2026 a group of its authorised users says the registered map wrongly takes in distant forests whose honey has none of Bansvan's qualities, and wants the entry corrected. Their lawyer plans to apply to the IPAB. What is the best advice?
quiz.ok: Seek rectification as planned, but the IPAB is gone, and such matters now go to the High Court.
no: Proceed as planned, since the IPAB still hears rectification matters about registered GIs.
Drop the claim, since a GI's map could be challenged only by opposing the application in time.
File a public interest petition in the High Court instead, since a wrong map harms the public.
quiz.why: Any person aggrieved can apply under section 27 to cancel or correct an entry in the register, for example because a GI was wrongly registered, so authorised users harmed by a wrongly drawn map can seek rectification long after the opposition period. Such matters used to go to the IPAB, but the Tribunals Reforms Act, 2021 abolished it, and appeals and rectification matters now go to the High Court, though an application can also be made to the Registrar. The public interest petition is the tempting wrong turn: in the Tirupati Laddu dispute the Madras High Court dismissed a PIL because a rectification application was the proper remedy.

quiz.concept: Five-year limit runs from knowledge
quiz.q: Hillview Hotels has run a bar called 'Darjeeling Corner' since 2014 and registered that name as a trade mark in 2017. The Tea Board learnt of the bar in March 2015, sent objection letters in 2016 and 2018, and sued in 2021; no bad faith is alleged. The Board argues that each day of continued use is a fresh wrong, so the five-year limit cannot defeat it. How should the court treat the argument?
quiz.ok: Reject it: time ran from the Board's knowledge in 2015, and neither the letters nor continued use restarted it
no: Accept it: continued use is a fresh wrong every day, so the suit is in time at least for current use
Accept it: the 2018 letter kept the Board's objection alive and started a fresh five-year period
Reject it: time ran from the day the bar opened in 2014, whatever the Board knew at that point
quiz.why: Under section 26(4), no action lies against the use or registration of a trade mark after five years from the date the GI owner came to know of it (or the date the mark was registered, if that came first and the mark had been published by then), unless there was bad faith. The Board knew in March 2015, so time ran out in March 2020 and the 2021 suit is late, just as the 2006 and 2008 letters in Tea Board v ITC did not save a suit filed in 2010. The continuing-wrong argument is the tempting one, but Tea Board v ITC rejected the idea that the period starts afresh each day the use continues.

quiz.concept: A GI covers goods, not services
quiz.q: A Pune events firm calls its wedding-planning service 'Kanchipuram Silk Weddings'. It sells and supplies no sarees; clients pay only for the planning. The registered proprietor of the Kanchipuram silk GI sues for infringement within months of learning of it. Applying the reasoning in Tea Board v ITC, is the claim likely to succeed?
quiz.ok: No, because the GI is tied to goods, and wedding planning is a service, which the infringement heads fit poorly
no: Yes, because a registered GI gives its proprietor control over every trade use of the place name
No, because a GI can be enforced only against goods of exactly the same kind as the goods it is registered for
Yes, because using a famous GI to promote any business is unfair competition in itself
quiz.why: Tea Board v ITC held that the Darjeeling GI covers tea, which is goods, while a hotel lounge is a service, so the statutory heads fitted poorly; a GI is tied to goods and is not a monopoly over a place name. A planning service that supplies no silk goods at all is in the same position as the lounge. The 'same kind of goods' option reaches the right result for the wrong reason: Chinar Agro shows that a registered GI can be enforced against a different kind of goods, so the real weakness is that a service is not goods at all.

quiz.concept: No-confusion reasoning in Tea Board
quiz.q: A Kolkata hotel names its café 'Darjeeling Terrace', and the Tea Board sues within a year of learning of it. On the reasoning in Tea Board v ITC, the Board's case looks weak. Which added fact would most help the Board?
quiz.ok: Staff tell guests the café is an official Tea Board outlet, and the menus carry the Board's logo
no: The café serves only genuine Darjeeling tea, bought directly from gardens registered as authorised users
The hotel has also applied to register 'Darjeeling Terrace' as a trade mark, over the Board's objection
The café has become one of Kolkata's best-known venues after heavy advertising across India
quiz.why: One of the three reasons in Tea Board v ITC was that there was no confusion: guests would not think the lounge was licensed by the Tea Board or that everything served there came from Darjeeling. Staff presenting the café as an official Tea Board outlet, with the Board's logo on the menus, attacks that reason directly by creating a false impression of a connection with the Board. Serving genuine Darjeeling tea only makes the name more truthful, and neither a trade mark application (ITC had one too) nor the café's own fame shows any confusion.

quiz.concept: Passing off by suggestion; foreign law
quiz.q: Assume Scotch whisky is not registered as a GI in India. An Indian distiller sells its own whisky as 'Silver Scot' and is sued for passing off. It argues that it never uses the word 'Scotch', and that the UK law defining Scotch whisky has no force in India. On the reasoning in the Red Scot case, how do the two arguments fare?
quiz.ok: Both fail: 'Scot' can suggest Scotch whisky, and the UK law serves only to show what 'Scotch' means
no: The word argument wins: passing off can be made out only where the exact protected name is used
The UK law argument wins: an Indian court may look only to Indian law to find what a name means
Both fail, because TRIPS makes the UK law on Scotch whisky directly binding on Indian courts
quiz.why: In Scotch Whisky Association v Golden Bottling (2006) the Delhi High Court restrained 'Red Scot' as passing off although Scotch whisky was not a registered GI in India: the objection was that 'Scot' suggested Scotch whisky, and the court relied on the UK Scotch Whisky Act, 1988 and the Scotch Whisky Order, 1990 to show what 'Scotch' means. 'Silver Scot' raises the same two points, so both arguments fail. The TRIPS option reaches the right result for the wrong reason: the UK law was not applied as binding law but relied on to show the name's meaning, in a passing off action that section 20(2) keeps open.

quiz.concept: Precedent weight of an ex parte decree
quiz.q: CIVC's Indian GI registration for CHAMPAGNE covers wine. A Nashik company sells a non-alcoholic apple drink as 'Champagne Fizz', defends the suit and argues that a wine GI cannot reach a soft drink. CIVC relies on Chinar Agro. How much does that decision help CIVC?
quiz.ok: It is on point, but as an ex parte decree it carries less weight on arguments never put to the court
no: It is conclusive, since the court ruled only after hearing every argument of the defendant in full
It is of no use, since a decree passed ex parte can never be cited as a precedent in a later case
It helps only on passing off, since an undefended suit cannot decide any claim of statutory infringement
quiz.why: In CIVC v Chinar Agro Fruit Products (2017) the Delhi High Court enforced CIVC's registered wine GI against non-alcoholic drinks, fruit beer and juices, so the decision is on point on its facts: a registered foreign GI got full protection even against a different kind of goods. But the defendant never appeared and the decree was ex parte, so it carries less weight on points that were never argued, such as the one now raised. Less weight is not no weight, so the 'of no use' option overstates the point, and nothing confines the decision to passing off: CIVC also argued infringement under section 22.

quiz.concept: Why police a GI on other goods
quiz.q: A student asks why CIVC sued Chinar Agro at all, since no one buying a non-alcoholic fruit drink called 'Champagne' would think it was wine from the Champagne region. Which concern best explains the suit?
quiz.ok: Unchecked use on other drinks risked turning 'Champagne' into a generic word in India
no: Buyers would take the fruit drink to be French wine, so the label misled them about origin
Its Indian registration covers every kind of drink, so any drink called Champagne falls within it
Fruit drinks are notified goods, so using the name on them infringes even if no one is misled
quiz.why: In CIVC v Chinar Agro Fruit Products (2017), CIVC argued infringement under section 22, passing off and the danger of the name becoming generic in India, and won a permanent injunction against non-alcoholic drinks, fruit beer and juices. Where no buyer is misled about origin, the genericness danger is the real harm: if 'Champagne' comes to be used freely on any fizzy drink it may become a common word, and a generic name cannot be registered as a GI (section 9). The 'misled about origin' option ignores the premise of the question, the registration covers wine only, and the only notified goods are wines and spirits, not fruit drinks.

quiz.concept: Place of making decides GI use
quiz.q: Snackwell is a registered authorised user of the Bikaneri Bhujia GI for its plant in Bikaner, but it also makes bhujia at a plant in Indore. Both are sold in identical packets marked 'Snackwell Bikaneri Bhujia'. The GI proprietor objects. Following the approach in Bikaji Foods, what is Snackwell's main problem?
quiz.ok: Its Indore bhujia is sold as the GI product, so it must clearly separate GI from non-GI goods
no: None, since its authorised-user status attaches to the company, so all its bhujia may carry the GI
None, since the GI protects the Bikaner recipe, so bhujia made to it anywhere may use the name
Its own brand must go, since a GI cannot appear on the same packet as a private trade mark
quiz.why: In Bikaji Foods v Desai Brothers the Delhi High Court, at the interim stage, required a clear distinction between GI and non-GI products and sent a Local Commissioner to check whether the bhujia was really made in Bikaner, because where the goods are made is the key fact in GI use. Snackwell's Indore bhujia is not made in the GI area, so selling it in the same 'Bikaneri Bhujia' packet presents it as the GI product. Authorised-user status covers goods from the area, not everything the company makes; a GI protects a place link rather than a recipe; and Bikaji itself used its own BIKAJI mark alongside the GI.

quiz.concept: A locus ruling leaves the merits open
quiz.q: A devotee wants to cancel a temple trust's GI for its prasadam on the ground that it hurts religious feelings. Her lawyer advises: 'Don't bother. In the Tirupati Laddu matter the Registry upheld a prasadam GI against exactly that objection.' How should the advice be assessed?
quiz.ok: It is wrong: that challenge failed on locus, so the religious objection was never decided on its merits
no: It is right: the Registry rejected the religious objection on its merits when it dismissed that challenge
It is wrong: she should skip rectification and file a public interest petition in the High Court instead
It is wrong: any person may seek rectification, so her standing cannot be questioned at all
quiz.why: On 30 July 2012 the Registry dismissed the rectification application against the Tirupati Laddu GI because the applicant was not a 'person aggrieved', so the objection under section 9(d) has never been decided on its merits: locus decided the case. The devotee's religious ground therefore remains arguable, though, as Practice Problem 3 notes, she must first show that she is a person aggrieved under section 27, which is where the Tirupati challenge failed. A public interest petition is no substitute: the one against the laddu was dismissed in 2010 because rectification was the proper remedy.

quiz.concept: GI area boundaries decide who benefits
quiz.q: Farmers in a district just outside a registered GI area grow the same rice variety by the same methods, and tasters cannot tell their rice from the GI rice. They start selling it under the GI name. Can they lawfully do so, and what is their proper course?
quiz.ok: No; the registered area decides who benefits, so their remedy is to challenge where its boundary lies
no: Yes; a GI protects a variety and a method of growing, so the same rice may carry the name anywhere
Yes, once they register as authorised users, which any grower of the same variety is free to do
No; a GI area can never cross a district or state line, so the boundary cannot be redrawn at all
quiz.why: The Basmati dispute shows that the boundaries of the GI area decide who benefits: Madhya Pradesh's districts were left out of APEDA's application, and its opposition and later challenge failed before the IPAB and the Madras High Court. Farmers outside the registered area cannot use the name just because their rice is identical, since a GI rests on the link with a place and authorised users must be producers of that area, so their route is to contest the boundary. The 'no crossing of state lines' option is wrong, as the Kolhapuri Chappal GI covers districts in both Maharashtra and Karnataka.

quiz.concept: Only proprietors and users can enforce
quiz.q: A foreign label sells sandals in Mumbai stores as 'Kolhapuri Luxe', made in Portugal. The GI's proprietors have not acted, so a consumer rights NGO files a public interest petition asking the High Court to declare infringement and stop the sales. What is the likely result?
quiz.ok: Dismissal, as GI rights are proprietary and only the proprietors or authorised users can enforce them
no: Relief, as a GI is a community right that any member of the public may enforce on its behalf
Relief, as a court may decide infringement in a public interest case whenever the proprietors stay inactive
Dismissal, as only the sandals' design is copied and a GI does not protect the design of goods
quiz.why: In the Prada Kolhapuri case the Bombay High Court dismissed a public interest petition, holding that GI rights are statutory and proprietary, that only the registered proprietor or authorised users can enforce them, and that infringement cannot be decided in a PIL; the proprietors stayed free to sue. The NGO is in the same position, even though 'Kolhapuri Luxe' on Portuguese sandals might well infringe if the proprietors sued. The design-only option misreads these facts: the name itself is used here, so the reason for dismissal is standing, not the name-versus-design point.

quiz.concept: A GI protects the name, not design
quiz.q: An Italian fashion house shows sandals closely modelled on Kolhapuri chappals at a show in Paris, then sells them in its Indian stores as the 'Riviera Slide', never using the word Kolhapuri; nothing on the sandals or in the stores refers to Kolhapur. The registered proprietors sue in India for GI infringement. Which point best answers the claim about the Indian sales?
quiz.ok: A GI protects the name or sign used on goods, not their design, and the name was never used
no: The sandals were first shown abroad, so Indian GI law cannot reach any later sale of them in India
Only authorised users, not the registered proprietors, have standing to sue for GI infringement
A GI protects designs only for notified goods, and footwear has not yet been notified
quiz.why: A GI protects the name or sign used on goods, not their design or shape, which is the central lesson of the Prada Kolhapuri episode. The Indian sales never use the word Kolhapuri, so there is no use of the GI to complain of, however close the design. The 'shown abroad' option fails for the Indian sales, because Indian GI law does not reach a fashion show abroad but does reach goods sold in India under the name; and the extra protection for notified goods concerns uses of the name, never designs.

quiz.concept: GI law reaches only sales in India
quiz.q: A European fashion house shows sandals called 'Kolhapuri Slides', made in Spain, at a show in Paris and sells them only in its European stores. The Kolhapuri Chappal proprietors want to sue in India under the GI Act. Which change in the facts would most clearly bring the Act into play?
quiz.ok: The fashion house starts selling the sandals in its Indian stores under the same name
no: The fashion house makes the sandals' design an even closer copy of the chappals
The Paris show, with the sandals and their name, is streamed live to viewers in India
The fashion house admits in public that its sandals were inspired by Kolhapuri chappals
quiz.why: The Prada episode teaches that Indian GI law does not reach a fashion show abroad unless goods are sold in India under the name, and that a GI protects the name used on goods, not their design. Selling Spanish-made 'Kolhapuri Slides' in Indian stores would be use of the GI on goods sold in India, which the proprietors could then challenge. A closer copy of the design, a broadcast of the show and an admission of inspiration, which Prada itself made, change neither point.

quiz.concept: Spirit GI allows imported raw materials
quiz.q: A distillers' group in an EU region makes whisky from barley imported from Canada; mashing, distillation and maturation all take place in the region, and the whisky's reputation is tied to the region. A rival argues that the name cannot be an EU GI because the grain is not local. Is the rival right?
quiz.ok: No: a spirit GI needs a stage of distillation or preparation in the area, not local raw materials
no: Yes: just as for a PDO, a spirit-drink GI requires the grain itself to be grown in the named area
No: imported grain is fine under every EU label, since only the final step need take place in the area
Yes: spirit drinks fall outside EU GI protection and rely only on national labelling rules
quiz.why: The EU label for spirit drinks needs a quality, reputation or other characteristic essentially attributable to the origin and at least one stage of distillation or preparation in the area; the raw materials can come from elsewhere. Irish Whiskey is the class example: distilled and matured in Ireland although not all its raw materials are Irish. The tempting 'every EU label' option over-generalises, because a PDO needs all steps of production in the area, so imported raw materials are fine for a spirit GI but not for every label.

quiz.concept: TSG protects a method, not a place
quiz.q: A producers' group in one member state registers a TSG for a traditional style of cheese. A dairy in another member state makes the cheese faithfully to the registered method and sells it under the TSG name. The group objects that the cheese is not made in its home region. Is the objection sound?
quiz.ok: No: a TSG protects a traditional recipe or method, not a link with a place, so it can be made anywhere
no: Yes: a TSG is the EU's strictest geographical label and ties every step of production to the home region
Yes: a TSG works like a PGI, so at least one step of production must happen in the home region
No: but only because the dairy's member state never opposed the TSG when it was registered
quiz.why: A TSG (Traditional Speciality Guaranteed) protects a traditional recipe or method and has no link with a place: production can happen anywhere, which is why the notes stress that a TSG is not a GI at all. A dairy elsewhere that follows the registered method may therefore use the TSG name. The 'works like a PGI' option merges two labels: the rule of at least one step in the area belongs to the PGI, not to the TSG.

quiz.concept: EU label follows the link, not the product
quiz.q: A wine from a small EU valley owes its character essentially to the valley's soil, climate and growers, and every step from grape to bottle happens there. Relying on the class note 'agriculture: PDO; wines, spirits: GI; food: PGI', a student says its producers can seek only the plain 'GI' label. What should the producers be told?
quiz.ok: They can seek a PDO, since the label turns on the strength of the link and PDO covers wine
no: They must use the plain GI label, since that label is reserved for all wines and spirit drinks
They can seek only a PGI, since wine counts as a food and every food takes the PGI label
They can seek a TSG, since a TSG suits a wine made by traditional methods in one valley
quiz.why: The class mapping is wrong: PDO and PGI both cover food, agricultural products and wine, and the plain 'GI' label is for spirit drinks only. Which label fits depends on the strength of the link: a PDO needs quality or characteristics essentially or exclusively due to the particular environment, with all steps of production in the area, and this wine meets both tests. The 'plain GI' option repeats the class error, and a TSG has no link with a place at all, so it could not protect the valley's name.

quiz.concept: PGI needs only one local step
quiz.q: Producers in a German valley make a smoked sausage. The pork comes from farms across Europe, but the curing and smoking, done by an old local method, happen in the valley, and the sausage's fame is tied to it. Which EU label can protect the valley's name, and why?
quiz.ok: A PGI, as one key step happens in the valley and the sausage's reputation is attributable to it
no: A PDO, as the sausage's fame is tied to the valley, where the smoking that defines it is done
A TSG, as what makes the sausage special is an old local method of curing and smoking
None, as an EU label needs the meat itself to come from animals raised in the named area
quiz.why: A PDO needs every step of production, processing and preparation in the area, with quality essentially or exclusively due to its environment, while a PGI needs a quality, reputation or other characteristic essentially attributable to the origin and at least one step in the area. The valley does the curing and smoking and gives the sausage its fame, but the pork comes from elsewhere, just as the meat for Westfälischer Knochenschinken, a PGI ham, may originate anywhere. A PDO fails because the raw material is not from the area, and a TSG protects a recipe with no link to a place, so it could not protect the valley's name.

quiz.concept: PDO versus PGI: strength of link
quiz.q: Two groups seek EU labels for lamb, and both specifications require animals to be reared for their whole lives, slaughtered and dressed in the area. The island group's area is a small island chain whose grazing gives the meat its character; the national group's area covers most of a large country whose lamb is known for its general quality and reputation. Why might the island group get a PDO but the national group only a PGI?
quiz.ok: The island lamb's quality is essentially due to its environment; the national link rests on general renown
no: The national group's rules must let animals be reared outside the area, as a PGI needs only one step there
PDO status is kept for small, closed areas such as island groups, whatever the product's link with them
The national area joins mainland and islands, and a PDO area must be a single unbroken stretch of land
quiz.why: Shetland Lamb (PDO) and Scotch Beef (PGI) follow the same rearing rule, with animals reared for their entire lives, slaughtered and dressed in the area; the difference lies in how strong and how specific the link with the place is. Shetland Lamb's quality is essentially due to the islands' particular environment, while Scotch Beef's link is with the quality and reputation of Scottish beef in general, and the two lamb groups mirror that contrast. The option saying the national group's rules must allow rearing outside the area misreads the PGI rule: a PGI needs at least one step in the area, but nothing stops a specification from requiring more, as both groups' rules do here.

quiz.concept: EU-wide craft GIs since 2025
quiz.q: In 2026, an association of glass makers from an Italian island town, whose name has so far been protected only by a regional law, wants protection across the whole EU. What should it be told?
quiz.ok: It can now seek EU-wide protection under the craft and industrial products regime, run by the EUIPO
no: It must rely on the regional law, since EU GI law still covers only food, wine and spirit drinks
It should apply for a PDO, since the glass owes its quality wholly to the island's long tradition
It should apply to the Commission under the single 2024 GI law, which now covers crafts as well
quiz.why: Until 2025, EU GI law covered only agricultural products, food, wine and spirit drinks, so craft names such as Murano glass and Solingen cutlery depended on national or regional laws. Since 1 December 2025, Regulation (EU) 2023/2411 has protected craft and industrial products across the EU through the EUIPO, so the association now has an EU-wide route. The 'single 2024 law' option is the trap: Regulation 2024/1143 unified wine, spirit drinks, agricultural products and TSG, while crafts sit under the separate 2023/2411 regime, and a PDO is for food, agricultural products and wine.

quiz.concept: Single producer applicant: EU versus India
quiz.q: In an Italian village, one family is the only remaining producer of a traditional essential oil and wants the village name protected in the EU. In an Indian village, one weaver is the only maker of a rare textile and wants an Indian GI for it. How do the two systems treat these applications?
quiz.ok: The EU can accept a sole producer in exceptional cases, but India requires a body representing producers
no: Both can accept them, since a GI turns on the link with the area, not on how many produce there
Neither can accept them, since a GI is a community right that a single producer may never seek
India can accept the weaver once she registers as an authorised user, but the EU always insists on a group
quiz.why: EU law allows a single producer to apply in exceptional cases, typically where that producer is the only one in the area, and the name then relates to that producer's village or area. Indian law has no such exception: section 11 allows an application only by an association, organisation or authority representing the producers. Registering as an authorised user is no way round this, because authorised users are entered in Part B against a GI that a representative body has registered in Part A.

quiz.concept: EU filing route: national or direct
quiz.q: Two applications reach the European Commission directly: one from a Kenyan tea growers' group and one from a Portuguese cheese group that skipped its national authority. Both are complete on their documents. Which is procedurally sound?
quiz.ok: Only the Kenyan one, since non-EU groups apply to the Commission while EU groups must start nationally
no: Only the Portuguese one, since non-EU groups must first apply through a member state's national authority
Both, since every application, from inside or outside the EU, now goes straight to the Commission
Neither, since every application must first pass a national opposition stage in some member state
quiz.why: In the EU, a producer group's application goes first to its own member state's national authority for scrutiny and a national opposition stage, and only then to the Commission, which examines it before publication and the 3 month EU opposition period. A group from a third country applies to the Commission directly, with its specification, a single document and proof that the name is protected at home. So the Kenyan filing is sound and the Portuguese one is not; the option that sends non-EU groups through a member state reverses the two routes.

quiz.concept: Commission's own check after national approval
quiz.q: An Italian producer group's application passes national scrutiny and the national opposition stage, and Italy sends it on to the European Commission. The Commission finds that the specification does not meet EU law. The group argues that, once a member state has approved an application, the Commission must publish the name. Is the group right?
quiz.ok: No: the Commission examines the application itself and may reject it if it fails EU law
no: Yes: the Commission's role is only to publish names that a member state has already approved
Yes: after national approval, only an opposition filed at the EU stage can still stop the name
No: the group should have gone straight to the Commission, as every EU producer group must
quiz.why: In the EU an application passes two filters: national scrutiny with a national opposition stage, and then the Commission, which examines the application and can reject it if it does not meet EU law, before publication in the Official Journal and a 3 month opposition period. National approval sends the application on but does not bind the Commission, so the group is wrong. The 'only an opposition' option skips the Commission's own examination, and the direct route to the Commission is for groups from outside the EU.

quiz.concept: EU sustainability practices are voluntary
quiz.q: An EU producer group's application names its control body and is otherwise complete. The group also wants to bind its members to environmental practices that go beyond what the law requires. Its adviser Rossi says the application will be refused unless it proves such practices; its adviser Weber says such practices cannot appear in the product specification at all. Who is right?
quiz.ok: Neither: such practices are voluntary, but the group may write them into the specification
no: Rossi: since 2024, every application must prove environmental, social and economic sustainability
Weber: a specification may set rules only on where and how the product itself is made
Each in part: such practices must be proved for food, but may not be included for wine
quiz.why: Under Regulation 2024/1143, producer groups may agree on a voluntary basis to sustainability practices that go beyond what the law requires, and these can be written into the product specification; they are not a compulsory filing requirement. What the application must contain is the control body that will check compliance, and this group has named one. Rossi repeats the class note that the applicant 'has to show' sustainability when filing, which the notes correct, and Weber overlooks that such practices may go into the specification.

quiz.concept: US rule: first in time, first in right
quiz.q: Suppose an Indian GI for 'Kesari Silk' sarees was registered in India in 2009. In 2012 a New Jersey company registered KESARI as a US trade mark for sarees it makes there. In 2026 the Indian proprietor applies for a US certification mark for the name. What is the likely result?
quiz.ok: Refusal, since the earlier US trade mark wins and priority among US rights decides the contest
no: Registration, since the GI was registered in India first and so is earlier in time than the US mark
Registration, since a certification mark for a GI always prevails over an ordinary trade mark
Refusal, since the US gives no protection of any kind to geographical indications from abroad
quiz.why: The US has no separate GI law and protects GIs through its trade mark system, where the key rule is first in time, first in right: the earlier right wins. An existing US trade mark for the same name therefore blocks a later certification mark application, which is the risk the classroom Kashmiri Kesar hypothetical illustrates. The Indian registration date does not help, because US strength depends on who registered first in the US system; and foreign GIs can be protected there, as Darjeeling tea is by a certification mark.

quiz.concept: US certification versus collective marks
quiz.q: A council in a US apple-growing valley grows and sells no apples itself. It wants any grower in the valley, member or not, whose apples meet its published standards to be able to use the valley's name, and it will police those standards. Which US tool fits best?
quiz.ok: A certification mark, as the council would certify origin and standards for any qualifying grower
no: A collective mark, as every grower in the valley would share the right as a member of one association
An ordinary trade mark, as the valley's name would come to identify the council's own business
A separate GI registration, as TRIPS obliges every member to keep its own register of GIs
quiz.why: In the US a certification mark lets its owner certify that goods come from the region and meet its standards (Darjeeling tea is protected this way), a collective mark is used by the members of a group or association, and an ordinary trade mark fits where a place name has come to identify one business. A council that sells nothing and opens the name to every qualifying grower, member or not, fits the certification model. The TRIPS option is wrong: TRIPS sets minimum standards but leaves each country free to choose the method, which is why the US needs no separate GI law.

quiz.concept: Evocation in the EU, priority in US
quiz.q: A dairy outside Italy sells hard cheese labelled 'Parmesan', with its true origin printed clearly on the pack, in both the EU and the US. How would the two systems approach the label?
quiz.ok: The EU bars it as evoking a protected name unless shown generic; in the US, earlier mark rights decide
no: Both allow it, since a label that states the true origin cannot mislead buyers in either market
Both bar it, since TRIPS obliges every member to stop evocation of any GI used for cheese
The US bars it as evocation, while the EU allows it unless buyers are shown to have been actually deceived
quiz.why: The EU gives the strongest protection, including against evocation: in the Parmesan case (2008) 'Parmesan' was held to evoke Parmigiano Reggiano, so it could not be used on cheese not made to the specification even with the true origin shown, and genericness had to be proved. The US has no separate GI law and works through trade marks, so the outcome there depends on who holds the earlier right under the first in time, first in right rule. No TRIPS rule bans evocation for cheese; its extra protection in Article 23 is for wines and spirits.

quiz.concept: Who may use the name: EU versus India
quiz.q: A new cheesemaker sets up inside the area of a registered EU name, follows the product specification in full and is checked by the control body. A new weaver sets up inside the area of a registered Indian GI and weaves exactly to the registered standards. Neither has joined the group or body that applied for the name. Who may use the name on their goods now?
quiz.ok: The cheesemaker, as the EU name is open to all who follow the specification; the weaver must first become an authorised user
no: Both, since each makes its goods inside the area and keeps exactly to the registered standards
Neither, since in both systems only members of the body that applied may ever use the name
The weaver, as any producer of the area may use an Indian GI at once; the cheesemaker must first join the applicant group
quiz.why: The notes' comparison of the three systems shows the difference. In the EU the producer group applies, but the name is protected for everyone who follows the specification; in India a producers' body registers the GI in Part A, and individual producers must apply under section 17 to be entered in Part B as authorised users, who alone may use the name. So the cheesemaker may use the EU name now, but the weaver must first register. The 'both' option applies the EU model to India, and the 'neither' option wrongly confines both systems to members of the applicant body.

quiz.concept: Choosing the defence that fits
quiz.q: 'Malaipak' has been the everyday name for a kind of coconut sweet across one southern state since the 1970s. In 2018 a producers' body from another state registers 'Malaipak' as a GI for its own sweet. A shop in the southern state, which uses 'Malaipak' only as the name of the sweets it makes and has no trade mark, is sued for infringement. Which defence on the problem-answer checklist fits best?
quiz.ok: The common-name defence, as the word was the ordinary name of such sweets in part of India
no: The prior trade mark defence, since the shop's use of the word began in good faith before the GI
The exhaustion defence, since the shop sells only genuine sweets that it has made for itself
The five-year limit, since the shop has used the word for more than five years without challenge
quiz.why: The problem-answer checklist lists five defences: exhaustion (section 22(4)), a prior good faith trade mark (section 26(1)), a common name (section 26(2)), own name (section 26(3)) and the five year limit (section 26(4)). Section 26(2) says the Act does not apply to a term that was the common name of the goods in any part of India on or before 1 January 1995, and 'Malaipak' has been the everyday name of the sweet in the southern state since the 1970s. The prior trade mark and five-year defences both need a trade mark, which the shop does not have, and exhaustion covers the resale of genuine GI goods, not a rival's own sweets.

quiz.concept: Passing off survives the five-year bar
quiz.q: A Kolkata café has traded as 'Darjeeling Brew House' since 2017 and registered that name as a trade mark in 2018. The Tea Board learnt of it in 2017 but did nothing until 2026, and there is no sign of bad faith. A junior concludes that the Board has no claim of any kind left. Which assessment is best?
quiz.ok: Passing off may still be argued, but the Board must prove that customers were deceived
no: An infringement suit is still open, since the limit protects the café's registration but not its use
Nothing survives, since the five-year limit bars every kind of action concerning the name
The extra protection for notified goods still applies, as it is not subject to the limit
quiz.why: Practice Problem 1 is in point. Section 26(4) bars action against the use or registration of a trade mark five years after the GI owner knew of it, unless there was bad faith, so a Board that knew in 2017 was out of time from 2022; the GI claim also fits a café poorly, because a café is a service. The suggested answer adds that passing off may still be argued, but the Board must then prove that customers were deceived, which is why the claim is weak rather than dead. The infringement option misreads the limit, which covers use as well as registration, and tea is not a notified good.
